To showcase model capabilities, we present simulations exhibiting different types of cellular dynamics produced when varying the mechanisms underlying apoptosis. The model is subsequently applied to probe different morphological transitions, such as cell shrinkage, membrane blebbing, cavity formation and fragmentation. Lastly, we compare the characteristics observed in our simulations to electron microscopy images, providing additional support for the model.

items.title: S1CogBench: What System One Decision Models Can and Cannot Do on Cognitive Experiments
items.summary: Decision-making in humans and AI involves multiple cognitive abilities. System One decision models produce fast, structured choices. Their cognitive strengths and limitations, however, remain poorly understood. We introduce S1CogBench, a benchmark of 24 established cognitive tasks and 27 evaluation modes, evaluating seven open models and the API model Jev. It combines human-response prediction, autonomous execution, and controlled task manipulations to reveal strengths and failures that aggregate scores miss. We find distinct behavioral profiles across the evaluated models. In these models, strong performance on some learning tasks coexists with failures to gather information or adapt to feedback, while high accuracy does not guarantee human-like responses to changing task demands. Shared readout controls show that model rankings depend partly on how choices are extracted. Separate latency comparisons with generative language models show that long responses are much slower than direct decisions, whereas matched one-token generation adds little overhead. To our knowledge, S1CogBench is the first benchmark of System One decision models on established cognitive experiments. It provides a common empirical basis for identifying their capabilities and limitations before integrating them into automated decision systems.

items.title: From Mutation to Medication: Characterizing Failures of Clinical LLMs to Respect Genomic Resistance
items.summary: Language models are increasingly proposed to support molecular tumour boards, but may recommend cancer therapies despite genomic evidence of resistance. We evaluated ten models on 1,464 resistance cases from five curated oncology knowledge bases, collecting 58,910 judgments. Models endorsed resisted therapies in 21.8-81.4% of cases. However, raw rates can reflect a tendency to agree rather than an ability to distinguish resistance from drug sensitivity: one open-weight model endorsed 81.4% of resistance cases and 82.3% of sensitivity controls. We therefore compared endorsement within matched gene and evidence-level groups. This analysis is exploratory because it was specified after the pre-registered analysis, which yielded null-to-weak results. Measured failures depended strongly on the reference knowledge base and evidence strength. When a second source independently confirmed resistance, four models across three vendors endorsed at most 2.4% of cases; at weaker evidence tiers, discrimination was not measurable. Models sometimes acknowledged resistance yet recommended the therapy. Repeating a model's own resistance conclusion reduced endorsement to 0.0-3.5% on cases where it had stated resistance. Falsely attributing the opposite conclusion increased endorsement above baseline for all seven hosted models, reaching 95.2% for GPT-4o; an instruction without an attributed conclusion changed endorsement by only 0.9 percentage points. Providing the correct curated evidence reduced unqualified strong recommendations to 0.3-3.5%, testing evidence use under an oracle condition rather than retrieval.

items.title: Generation of protein conformations using a simple inverted transformer
items.summary: Molecular dynamics is an extremely powerful approach for studying protein behavior, but it requires enormous computational resources to obtain an adequate sampling of possible conformations. Recently, thanks to successes in predicting three-dimensional protein structures, there has been an explosion of research exploring the opportunities offered by deep learning to address the problem of protein conformational landscape. In this work, an artificial intelligence system based on a variant of the Transformer architecture is introduced and applied to the problem of determining the ensemble of three-dimensional structures that a protein can access and their statistical weight. After being trained on a dataset of conformations of a particular protein obtained using classical all-atom molecular dynamics, this neural network is able to directly generate physically plausible protein conformations similar to those obtained both through molecular dynamics and experimentally. The ordered sequence of conformations obtained as output of the neural network rapidly converges towards the most populated regions of the protein's conformational landscape, suggesting that the system may have learned not only the protein's three-dimensional organization but also the thermodynamic weights of the various feasible conformations. These features, combined with its simplicity and low computational load, make this Transformer variant an ideal candidate for the development of systems capable of performing generative molecular dynamics.

items.title: Arginine metabolism drives tumor immune escape by shaping an immunosuppressive microenvironment
items.summary: The tumor microenvironment evolves through the ``elimination-equilibrium-escape'' paradigm, yet the quantitative mechanisms by which metabolic reprogramming contributes to immune evasion remain unclear. We develop a mathematical model of tumor-immune interactions to investigate how arginine metabolism shapes an immunosuppressive microenvironment. We establish the positivity and boundedness of solutions and analyze the existence and stability of equilibrium states. The model is calibrated using tumor growth data from three mouse cohorts and reproduces tumor growth patterns under distinct immune conditions. The calibrated model predicts faster tumor growth in immunocompetent mice than in immunodeficient controls, with macrophage dynamics accounting for this difference. It further predicts that arginine administration promotes tumor progression by enhancing macrophage polarization and weakening T cell-mediated tumor control. To account for interindividual heterogeneity, we develop the TVInfABC algorithm to generate a virtual mouse cohort. Moreover, our analysis indicates that tumor-associated macrophages can promote transitions from immunologically ``hot'' to ``cold'' states. Systematic pharmacodynamic simulations further uncover a synergy between arginine depletion (anti-ARG1) and immune checkpoint blockade (anti-PD-1/PD-L1). These results provide a mathematical basis for studying metabolic-immune interactions and for evaluating mechanism-based combination therapies.

items.title: A unified cross-scale framework for the dynamic Waddington landscape
items.summary: The Waddington epigenetic landscape is a foundational concept in developmental biology, yet its quantitative formulations remain largely disconnected from the population dynamics that originally motivated the metaphor. Existing approaches typically describe either intracellular gene-regulatory dynamics or population-level cell kinetics, but rarely both within a unified framework. Here, we develop a unified PDE-integral framework that couples stochastic gene-regulatory dynamics with probability-conserving population renewal, yielding a dynamic Waddington landscape $U(\vec{x}, t) = -\log f(\vec{x}, t)$ defined directly from the evolving epigenetic probability density $f(\vec{x}, t)$. Rigorous mathematical analysis of this framework establishes its well-posedness and provides conditions for the existence and uniqueness of stationary solutions. Application to canonical gene regulatory circuits shows that proliferation is not merely a determinant of population size, but an active regulator of landscape topology. Population renewal reshapes attractor stability and transition barriers in a circuit-dependent manner, generating transient plasticity in some regulatory architectures while stabilizing progenitor states in others. Under highly proliferative conditions, these interactions further produce oscillatory ``breathing'' landscapes. Together, these results establish population renewal as an integral component of cell-fate regulation and extend the Waddington landscape from a static description of intracellular dynamics to a predictive multiscale framework linking gene regulation, cell-state dynamics, and tissue homeostasis.

items.title: Simulated Annealing with Topological Spatial Chunking for De Novo Protein Sequence Design
items.summary: The inverse protein folding problem, designing a discrete amino acid sequence that spontaneously folds into a predefined macroscopic structure, remains a phenomenally demanding combinatorial challenge central to synthetic drug discovery. While algorithms like SA offer a baseline approach for navigating dense biomolecular energy landscapes, applying SA heuristics to large sequences is inherently frustrated by exponentially large search spaces and deep local energy minima. This study proposes a scalable sequence design architecture, Topological Spatial Chunking Simulated Annealing, based on a localized, exact-solving heuristic embedded within a global simulated-annealing wrapper. To fundamentally circumvent exponential scaling walls, we deploy a dynamic solver that segments the global molecular target into shallow, k-variable algorithmic windows. Crucially, rather than partitioning natively by sequential 1D chronology, we introduce topological spatial chunking, which dynamically groups discrete variables based on Euclidean spatial proximity to preserve critical non-local thermodynamic correlations. The spatially localized sub-problems are solved deterministically via exact enumeration, while the global traversal is securely regulated by an exterior simulated annealing governor augmented by dynamic reheating and continuous elitism caching. We comprehensively benchmarked this classical architecture on the standard HP biophysical lattice against targeted 20-merA, 25-mer, 50-mer, and 64-mer geometries. Most notably, when evaluating the computationally exhaustive 50-mer and 64-mer topologies, the framework successfully bypassed widely accepted heuristic boundaries. By leveraging deterministic exact solving to vault classical energy traps, the system algorithmically resolved a novel, ultra-dense sequence-packing configuration for the 50-mer, defining a new theoretical global optimum.

items.title: Midsagittal Corpus Callosum Parameterization: A Framework for Spatially Detailed Diffusion MR Imaging Analysis
items.summary: The corpus callosum (CC) is the largest white matter structure in the human brain and plays a central role in interhemispheric communication. Diffusion MR imaging is widely used to investigate microstructural organization, but commonly used analysis approaches have important limitations. Voxel-based methods rely heavily on accurate inter-subject registration and smoothing choices, tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) restricts the analysis to a narrow white matter skeleton, and parcellation approaches reduce spatial detail by averaging diffusion measures over relatively large regions. In this work, we introduce a parameterization framework for the analysis of the midsagittal CC that resamples the structure using a standardized grid of points, establishing a geometric correspondence across individuals without explicit inter-subject registration. In a test-retest dataset, the method provided stable measurements while covering most of the midsagittal CC, and sensitivity analyses showed that results in the central CC changed little under perturbations of the input CC mask, whereas peripheral regions were more sensitive. The framework was further evaluated in group analyses of aging and Alzheimer's disease in datasets that differ in acquisition protocol and spatial resolution. Effect-size maps and quantitative comparisons showed that its results were largely consistent with TBSS and parcellation-based analyses in the overall spatial pattern of effects, while also revealing additional spatially localized differences. These findings suggest that the parameterization provides a simple, computationally efficient, and spatially detailed approach for investigating midsagittal CC microstructure, offering a structure-specific complement to whole-brain and region-based methods.

items.title: Match and Correct: A Repeated Computational Motif in Evoformer Layers
items.summary: Triangle attention and triangle multiplicative updates form key components of the Evoformer, and were introduced specifically to encourage consistency with the triangle inequality. Yet whether representational changes over layers reduce triangle inequality violations has not been tested. We probe the pair representation at each of OpenFold's 48 Evoformer layers, decoding final C$_α$-C$_α$ distances with four probe families (a shared linear probe, per-protein linear probes, a sequence-separation-gated linear probe, and XGBoost) and reconstructing intermediate 3D structures from the decoded distances via multidimensional scaling. Across a cohort of 552 CAMEO and ECOD proteins, distance decodability ($R^2$) and reconstruction quality (TM-score) rise in early layers, plateau in the middle of the network, and rise again in late layers. Directly measuring triangle-inequality violations in the decoded distances reveals a similar, more exaggerated pattern: violations rise to a peak, fall to a trough, rise to a second peak, and only then decline, revealing two distinct episodes of decreasing normalized triangle violations rather than one continuous improvement. Cumulative forward and reverse layer-wise ablations of the Pair Transition, MSA Transition, and triangle mechanisms localize the regions in which specific Evoformer components become essential. The two stages of geometric refinement coincide with the use of the Pair Transition MLP and the triangle mechanisms. These results characterize how distance information and decoded geometric consistency evolve across layers, and motivate hypotheses about the computations behind their trajectories.

items.title: A Structural Theory of Admissible Transitions in Biological Reaction Networks
items.summary: Biological reaction networks exhibit transient changes that cannot be understood from steady states or long-term persistence alone. We extend Chemical Organization Theory to transitions between species subsets, using stoichiometry and feasible reaction fluxes to characterize structurally admissible changes without specifying kinetic parameters. The framework distinguishes algebraic admissibility from feasibility constrained by reactant availability. We relate these transitions to reaction-based ordinary differential equations and identify an asymmetry: closure-building transitions are determined by network structure, whereas subsequent reductions can depend on the realized trajectory. Transitions to terminal organizations are characterized when the relevant species sets occur along that trajectory. An HIV-immune response model illustrates how a shared closure-building phase can precede different long-term outcomes. The framework connects continuous dynamics with discrete changes in species composition and supports structural analysis of transient pathways and organization formation in systems biology, while distinguishing structural admissibility from realization under particular kinetics.

items.title: Multi-Assay Antibody Developability Prediction with Shared Structure-Language Representations
items.summary: Early assessment of antibody developability is critical in drug discovery, but computational approaches remain limited by the scarcity of experimental data. We explore two strategies for working within that limit. First, we designed per-residue physicochemical descriptors encoding the local structural environment, including new terms such as directional charge asymmetry and screened electrostatic potential. These feed a convolutional network, combined with protein language model (PLM) embeddings in a two-stream architecture: the two are encoded and predicted independently and merged only at the prediction stage. Second, a shared trunk with per-assay heads passes information between related assays. Both are implemented in the Multi-Assay Developability Model (MADM) and evaluated on eight assays: HIC, heparin affinity (HAC), AC-SINS, and polyspecificity ELISA against BVP, dsDNA, insulin, ovalbumin and soluble membrane proteins (SMP), with labels from 29 open sources. Structural descriptors match or exceed PLM embeddings (AbLang2, ESM2) on several assays; combining the streams gives a small but consistent gain in accuracy and reduces seed-to-seed variance. Multi-assay training raises Spearman rho for ovalbumin and SMP by about 0.1, where assays correlate and share sequence space. Under cluster-split cross-validation the strongest results are for HAC, ovalbumin, insulin, SMP and HIC (rho = 0.70-0.82); AC-SINS, BVP and dsDNA are weaker (0.50-0.55). In these three, sequence clusters largely coincide with data source, so a held-out fold measures transfer to differently calibrated measurements as well as to new sequences. On the 80-antibody GDPa3 hold-out, performance falls by rho around 0.1 for all but SMP (0.22). Transfer to the VHH panel of Ginkgo GDPa5 gives comparable results, and scFv validation against binary SMP labels yields F1 = 0.89, AUC = 0.95.

items.title: FETTUCCINE: Fast and efficient brain-to-text decoding on mobile devices
items.summary: Recent advances in speech neuroprostheses have enabled new communication avenues for people who have lost the ability to speak due to neurological illness or injury. These systems can decode neural activity during attempted speech into text by relying on language priors to achieve high decoding accuracy. This performance currently comes at the cost of using a compute-intensive language modeling stack, presenting a major bottleneck for real-world use. Further, current language models incur highly variable and disruptive inference latencies, limiting communication throughput and preventing users from reliably participating in natural conversation. We introduce FETTUCCINE, an end-to-end brain-to-text framework that leverages the speed and portability of automatic speech recognition (ASR) models to address the aforementioned practical challenges, while achieving usable (<10%) word error rates (WER), efficient adaptation to neural non-stationarities, and reliable performance on mobile devices. When evaluated using publicly available data from an intracortical speech neuroprosthesis user, FETTUCCINE outperforms previous end-to-end methods, achieving as low as 4.39% WER. Most notably, our models successfully run on a commercially-available mobile device with throughput reaching up to 370x real-time, providing the first demonstration of brain-to-text decoding on a mobile device. We also show that our models can be successfully finetuned to extend usable performance to future days. Beyond performance, our approach enables localization of the neural features most relevant for decoding via gradient-based saliency maps, which we show align with well-established physiological priors across different ASR model families. Taken together, our results show that FETTUCCINE overcomes core infrastructural and computational barriers, yielding a new class of portable brain-to-text communication.

items.title: Learning Task-Specific Antibody Representations via Function-Aware Masking
items.summary: Antibody-specific language models pretrained via masked language modeling (MLM) learn representations that are critical for downstream sequence design and property prediction tasks. Yet, the corruption process itself is rarely leveraged as a source of inductive bias during pretraining. While preferentially masking complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) improves binding-related predictions, antibodies possess diverse biological priors over a variety of functions. Herein, we introduce function-aware masking, a family of pretraining algorithms that align mask placement with specific functional priors (e.g., from IMGT annotations or structure predictions) to shape the learned representation space. We show that these specialist masking strategies significantly improve performance on their respective objectives, yielding up to a 14% gain on structure-related tasks and up to a 5.9x improvement on CDR-related tasks. To further improve performance across multiple functional axes, we develop hybrid masking strategies that integrate multiple priors, balancing reconstruction over binding, structural, and biophysical objectives. Our results demonstrate that informed mask placement provides a parameter-free mechanism for imposing functional inductive biases in antibody language model training.

items.title: Functional nestedness of soil nematode communities across Europe: integrating morphological counts and eDNA reads
items.summary: 1. Soil nematodes occupy multiple trophic positions and contribute to key processes in soil food webs. Their communities vary across land uses and environmental conditions, yet it remains unclear whether these differences mainly reflect taxon replacement or nested patterns of taxon occurrence. 2. Here, we analysed two independent European datasets of soil nematode communities, SOB4ES, based on eDNA metabarcoding, and NemEu, based on morphological identification, to examine how genus composition varies across land uses. We partitioned community dissimilarity into turnover and nestedness-resultant components and compared sites under contrasting land uses with those sharing the same land use, while accounting for geographical and soil-related variation. We also assessed matrix-level nestedness, differences among trophic groups and associations between genus composition and environmental gradients. 3. In both datasets, genus turnover was consistently greater between contrasting land uses than within the same land use. Although the differences were modest, they remained significant after accounting for geographical distance and genus richness, whereas nestedness-resultant dissimilarity contributed little to land-use differentiation. These findings suggest that land-use-associated differences in European nematode communities are expressed primarily through changes in genus identity rather than nested patterns of taxon occurrence. 4. The consistency of this result across independently assembled datasets supports the broader relevance of taxonomic turnover for understanding soil biodiversity patterns across European land uses.

items.title: Engineering Yeast Cells to Facilitate Information Exchange
items.summary: Although continuous advances in theoretical modelling of Molecular Communications (MC) are observed, there is still an insuperable gap between theory and experimental testbeds, especially at the microscale. In this paper, the development of the first testbed incorporating engineered yeast cells is reported. Different from the existing literature, eukaryotic yeast cells are considered for both the sender and the receiver, with α-factor molecules facilitating the information transfer. The use of such cells is motivated mainly by the well understood biological mechanism of yeast mating, together with their genetic amenability. In addition, recent advances in yeast biosensing establish yeast as a suitable detector and a neat interface to in-body sensor networks. The system under consideration is presented first, and the mathematical models of the underlying biological processes leading to an end-to-end (E2E) system are given. The experimental setup is then described and used to obtain experimental results which validate the developed mathematical models. Beyond that, the ability of the system to effectively generate output pulses in response to repeated stimuli is demonstrated, reporting one event per two hours. However, fast RNA fluctuations indicate cell responses in less than three minutes, demonstrating the potential for much higher rates in the future.

items.title: Emergent intercellular contact-force networks shaped by deformability
items.summary: We present a numerical study of contact-force organization in dense assemblies of active, deformable cells. Using the Fourier Contour Cell model, which enables efficient simulation of large cell deformations, we investigate how cell deformability and active motility shape spatial organization of intercellular forces. We find that, in the soft liquid regime at intermediate self-propulsion strength, the contact-force distribution becomes bimodal, reflecting the emergence of a distinct population of weak interactions. Persistent-homology analysis further reveals a characteristic force-network structure in which weak tip-tip interactions are enclosed by loops of strong side-side interactions. Simulations with elongated but non-deformable cells demonstrate that both the bimodal force distribution and the associated network motif require cell deformability rather than elongated cell shape per se. Furthermore, introducing a curvature constraint shows that local cell curvature regulates the strength of weak tip-tip interactions. Together, these results demonstrate that cell deformability and local geometric constraints can organize force transmission across dense active cellular assemblies.

items.title: Bayesian Comparison of Covid Origins Hypotheses
items.summary: Applying standard Bayesian methods to the most reliably known unclassified facts about the Covid epidemic allows crude estimation of the odds for research-related vs. purely zoonotic origins. Here a broadly inclusive zoonotic hypothesis is compared with a rather specific subset of the research-related hypothesis defined by known prior work and grant proposals. The important observations are the type of virus, the city of the first outbreak, the lack of known prior hosts, the anomalous early pattern of evolution, and two specific features of the viral sequence. The resulting odds strongly favor research. The odds remain fairly strong under inclusion of uncertainties in prior odds.

items.title: Lightweight Semantic EEG Foundation Model for Frozen Cross-Disorder Transfer
items.summary: Large-scale EEG foundation models have demonstrated promising transferability across neurological disorders, but often require millions of parameters and substantial computational resources. In this paper, we present the Universal Semantic EEG Foundation Model (USE-FM), a lightweight EEG foundation model that learns transferable neural representations through self-supervised signal reconstruction on the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus (TUEG). After pretraining, the encoder is frozen and evaluated on two clinically distinct downstream tasks, abnormal EEG detection (TUAB) and epileptic seizure recognition (TUEP), using a unified frozen-transfer protocol against recent EEG foundation models, including LUNA-Base and CBraMod. With only 1.46 million parameters, approximately one-fifth the size of existing models, USE-FM achieves competitive overall performance, including strong sensitivity and F1-score on TUEP (SEN $75.00 \pm 14.14$, F1 $70.37 \pm 4.01$), while maintaining competitive performance on TUAB (AUC $85.24 \pm 5.61$). Beyond downstream classification, latent representation analysis using $k$-means clustering together with PCA and t-SNE demonstrates that USE-FM learns organized semantic EEG representations comparable to substantially larger foundation models. These results suggest that large-scale self-supervised pretraining enables lightweight architectures to learn transferable semantic EEG representations, providing a computationally efficient foundation for cross-disorder analysis and future clinical decision support in neurological disorders.

items.title: PINR-ESI: Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Implicit Neural Representation Framework for EEG Extended-Source Imaging
items.summary: EEG extended-source imaging aims to localize active cortical regions and characterize their extent, yet supervised inverse networks typically depend on synthetic EEG-source pairs and may be sensitive to synthetic-to-real mismatch. We propose a physics-informed self-supervised implicit neural representation (INR) framework for spatial source reconstruction without paired source labels or simulation-based supervised pretraining. The lead-field matrix encodes the source-to-sensor volume-conduction model and constrains the INR through agreement between predicted and measured EEG. Cortical current density is represented as a continuous coordinate-based neural field. Forward EEG prediction samples the field at cortical vertices and applies local smoothing before lead-field mapping. A classical inverse estimate provides warm initialization and observation-specific spatial guidance through prior-guided support regularization. Simulations across varying SNRs, source extents, and source counts showed low spatial dispersion and good localization performance. Quantitative evaluation on clinical EEG recordings from epilepsy patients and qualitative analysis of scalp EEG during intracranial stimulation supported feasibility for real-world source imaging. These findings suggest the potential of physics-informed self-supervised INR for extended-source imaging.

items.title: A Variational Latent Equilibrium for Learning in Neuronal Circuits
items.summary: Brains remain unrivaled in their ability to recognize and generate complex spatiotemporal patterns. While AI is able to reproduce some of these capabilities, deep learning algorithms remain largely at odds with our current understanding of brain circuitry and dynamics. This is prominently the case for backpropagation through time (BPTT), the go-to algorithm for learning complex temporal dependencies. In this work we propose a general formalism to approximate BPTT in a controlled, biologically plausible manner. Our approach builds on, unifies and extends several previous approaches to local, time-continuous, phase-free spatiotemporal credit assignment based on principles of energy conservation and extremal action. Our starting point is a prospective energy function of neuronal states, from which we calculate real-time error dynamics for time-continuous neuronal networks. With this, as a first contribution we provide a simple and straightforward derivation of the adjoint method dynamical equations, the time-continuous equivalent to BPTT. Importantly, additional approximations are necessary to avoid unphysical temporal non-localities. One such approximation was recently proposed in Generalized Latent Equilibrium (GLE), but enforcing temporal locality of the backpropagating dynamics induces an error in the gain that becomes problematic when processing complex signals. Thus, our second contribution is to design a learning rule for the backward weights to find a fully local (in space and time) set of equations for neuron and synapse dynamics that corrects for this gain difference. With this inclusion of backward weight learning, our theory provides a rigorous framework for spatiotemporal deep learning in the brain, while simultaneously advancing a blueprint for physical circuits capable of carrying out these computations.

items.title: From life-history model to theories of ecological diversity: the impact of Madhav Gadgil's work
items.summary: In this article, we review and provide perspectives on the foundational contributions of the renowned ecologist Madhav Gadgil, including the Gadgil-Bossert life-history model, ecological diversity, population biology, harvesting theory, human-ecological systems, co-evolution, adaptive management, and environmental democracy. We take the Gadgil-Bossert model of reproductive allocation as a starting point for reviewing Gadgil's broader contributions to evolutionary and population theory. Then we examine how density regulation shapes selection on reproductive allocation in his work on $r$- and $K$-selection. We then consider how interactions among genotypes determine whether a mixture can remain stable and resist invasion. We outline the key theoretical developments arising from these works and discuss their continued influence on contemporary ecological thought and present-day ecological systems.

items.title: CARVE: A glycan-specific framework for assessing protein-glycan binding-pose quality
items.summary: Protein-glycan interactions depend on the precise three-dimensional arrangement of carbohydrates at protein-binding interfaces, yet reliable assessment of predicted complex structures remains challenging. Existing evaluations commonly rely on fixed root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) thresholds, which do not fully account for the structural diversity and conformational flexibility of glycans. Here we developed CARVE, a glycan-specific framework for evaluating protein-glycan structure predictions. Through topology-aware glycan parsing, CARVE integrates orientation RMSD (oRMSD), interface-ring RMSD (irRMSD) and the fraction of native contacts (Fnat) to assess glycan scaffold geometry, interface-ring placement and native-contact recovery. These descriptors define four quality categories (CARVE-Level) with geometric thresholds that scale with the degree of polymerization (DP), and a continuous CARVE-Score, which reproduced those categories on 25,068 independently generated poses without recalibration (macro-F1 = 0.892). Pairing these measures with glycan-specific topological, chemical and geometric validity checks, we benchmarked nine prediction methods on CARVE-Bench, comprising 1,974 experimentally determined protein-glycan complexes. Among the top 25 predictions per target, HADDOCK3 achieved the highest Acceptable-level success rate (47.0%), whereas no method produced a high-quality, structurally valid pose for more than one in five. Collectively, CARVE provides a standardized basis for assessing protein-glycan structure prediction methods and guiding the development of more accurate docking and co-folding approaches.

items.title: Pragmatic Deeply Debiased ML
items.summary: Debiased machine learning (DML) combines a fitted outcome regression with weighted residuals to remove first-order regularization bias when estimating parameters such as average treatment effects, yet a second-order bias remains whenever regression and weighting errors align. For linear regression functionals, we target this second-order bias by training a strong learner to predict first-stage residuals from many covariates, yielding a one-dimensional (or low-dimensional) working model whose bias contribution is estimated on an independent sample. To complement this targeted search, we also analyze general kernel-based corrections, including covariate partitions and smoothers. We prove that deeply debiased ML is algebraically identical to ordinary DML evaluated with a post-hoc regression update that adjusts each scored observation using kernel-weighted residuals from the remaining evaluation observations. In our empirical and simulation studies, strong initial DML learners often leave the second-order correction small relative to sampling uncertainty, in which case the correction serves as a diagnostic check alongside sensitivity bounds for any remaining misspecification bias.

items.title: Non-Invariance in Nested Prediction Models under Selective Predictor Availability
items.summary: We use nested models as a framework for characterising the consequences of a selectively measured predictor in clinical prediction models. In this framework, a model containing predictors available in the target population is referred to as the restricted model, while the extended model additionally includes a selectively measured predictor. We show that non-invariance in the restricted model between selected patients and the target population decomposes into components due to omission of the additional predictor, potential residual non-invariance, and their interaction, and that it requires selection through manifestations of the disease process beyond the restricted-model predictors. We further show that imputation based on the conditional distribution of the additional predictor in the selected population transfers the restricted-model non-invariance to the imputed extended model as imputation bias. We propose diagnostic tests for selective measurement and restricted-model non-invariance that can be applied to routinely collected data, and illustrate the framework using publicly available intensive care data, in which blood lactate is selectively measured. A simulation study with binary and time-to-event outcomes illustrates these results and evaluates the diagnostic tests in finite samples. The framework provides a formal basis for understanding how selective predictor measurement affects generalisability of clinical prediction models using routinely collected health data.

items.title: Certifying total-variation contamination by betting on trimmed kernel witnesses
items.summary: Two laws share a common component after each discards a fraction $α$ of its mass, a trimming, exactly when their total variation is at most $α$, so the contamination level $α^\star = \mathrm{TV} (P,Q)$ is the share of each population without counterpart in the other. We bound it from below from two samples on any space with a bounded characteristic kernel. The kernel mean embeddings of all such trimmings of a law form a convex region, the regions of two laws first touch at $α^\star$, and in every direction a region reaches as far as a trimmed mean. The difference of their closest points, the witness, selects the trimming. We fit a ramp of the witness on part of the data and bet on the rest, at each level of a grid. The bound is valid at every sample size. The cut points of the tested level carry most of its finite-sample gain over an untrimmed witness, while refitting the witness at that level makes it consistent, gives its rates and returns the trimming. When a function of the kernel's Hilbert space separates the parts of the two laws without counterpart, the bound is within order $(n\wedge m)^{-1/2}$ of $α^\star$ on a grid of that mesh, which is minimax over such pairs. When these parts touch, a margin condition guarantees a polynomial rate for Sobolev kernels and a logarithmic rate for the Gaussian kernel. For the Laplace kernel on the line this guarantee is not sharp: the witness stays between its two cut points, and for densities that cross once, with a likelihood ratio bounded away from one off the crossing, the error on such a grid is again of that order up to logarithmic factors. No informative upper bound exists without assumptions. On the Right Heart Catheterization data, with confidence $0.95$, each arm must lose more than a fraction $0.35$ of its patients, if both lose the same fraction, before their covariate distributions can coincide.

items.title: Exact local queries for pseudo-marginal Markov chains
items.summary: Local queries of a Markov chain can depend on past updates outside the queried components. For pseudo-marginal chains with Gaussian graph priors, we construct decision certificates from finite historical parameter ranges to settle updates before all neighbouring records are resolved. Under shared random inputs and exact arithmetic, the executor recovers the reference parameters, auxiliary variables and likelihood estimates for any prespecified finite query sequence. We bound conditional expected work, including likelihood evaluation, historical range construction and execution management. On specified path and grid families, we fix per-node history lengths and all other parameters in the work bounds. As graph size grows, expected incremental work stays bounded for certificate execution and grows linearly for the specified cached pointwise evaluator answering the same query. In controlled experiments, certificate execution is faster than pointwise and parallel Picard execution for sparse queries, whereas Picard is faster than certificate execution for full queries. We apply the method to positron emission tomography and Gaussian process classification of Landmine data. For a fixed numerical tomography posterior, certificate execution completes all queries of regional mean distribution volume within budget, while full execution completes none from the same initial cache. In Landmine, posterior summaries of the difference in log length scales between two sites agree across pseudo-marginal and ancillary augmentation samplers within estimated Monte Carlo uncertainty. Certificate execution resolves almost every scheduled update over the full query sequence.

items.title: Statistical Process Monitoring of Functional Linear Models
items.summary: Monitoring the stability over time of the relationship between a functional response and multiple functional covariates is important in many industrial applications, either because the relationship itself is the quality characteristic of interest or because it underpins a predictive model whose validity must be verified as the process evolves. Existing methods either assume the model estimated in Phase I to be stable and monitor the resulting residuals, or re-estimate its coefficients at each sampling stage, which requires several observations to be available at a time. In this article, we propose the regression coefficient function (RCF) control chart to monitor functional linear models (FLMs) in which, at each sampling stage, an individual observation of the functional response and an arbitrary number of functional covariates become available. The proposed method employs an exponentially weighted moving loss to sequentially update estimates of the regression coefficient functions and the intercept function, which are monitored through Hotelling's $T^2$ and squared prediction error (SPE) control charts. A post-signal diagnostic procedure is also provided to support the identification of the source of the detected change. A Monte Carlo simulation study demonstrates that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly against small and persistent shifts, and a case study on monitoring the relationship between the air/fuel ratio and engine state variables in an automotive after-treatment system illustrates its practical applicability.

items.title: Generalizing Couple-Randomized Trials Under Limited Overlap and Missing Partner Linkage
items.summary: We study how to generalize couple-randomized trials when some couple types are absent from the trial and the target survey reports partner characteristics without linking spouses. Under an additive effect model with unrestricted partner-profile terms, the target average effect is identified exactly when the wife and husband margins assign equal mass to each connected component of the trial support graph. A specified interaction is identified when its alternating contrast around at least one cycle is nonzero. Without linkage, we obtain sharp bounds by optimizing over pairings consistent with the survey margins. A spousal odds ratio can narrow the bounds for a binary interaction. We derive joint bounds for an index-patient design, quantify bias from common shortcuts, and estimate effects and bounds using Bayesian dyadic multilevel regression and poststratification. In a worked example based on 3,826 Health and Retirement Study couples and simulated trial outcomes, an index-patient trial and an unlinked survey yielded a 2.93 mmHg wide identified set for the couple-average effect. Linking the survey narrowed it to 2.38 mmHg. Adding 300 couples without diabetes narrowed the unlinked set to 0.28 mmHg and yielded point identification with linkage under the fitted model.

items.title: Regression calibration for logistic regression with correlated measurement error and multiple misclassification in covariates
items.summary: Epidemiological analyses often suffer from covariate data quality issues: measurement error in continuous predictors and misclassification of categorical variables. Existing logistic regression correction methods mostly handle only one error type or a single misclassified variable, with limited tools for multiple misclassified categorical exposures together with correlated measurement error in continuous covariates. To address this gap, we extend regression calibration for logistic regression to jointly accommodate multiple continuous covariates with correlated additive measurement error and two or more misclassified categorical predictors. We build a unified framework integrating additive measurement error models and misclassification transition matrices, deriving the regression calibration estimator (RCE) using Kronecker product algebra. This computationally feasible approach extends naturally to more than two misclassified categorical variables. We evaluate RCE via simulations across varied misclassification rates, error magnitudes, sample sizes and effect sizes, comparing it with the naive estimator that ignores measurement error. We apply RCE to the EPIC-InterAct male case-cohort data to adjust for correlated error in protein and energy intake, plus misclassification in binary physical activity and three-category alcohol consumption. Results show that neglecting these error sources produces substantial bias and misleading inference for main and interaction effects in nutritional epidemiology. While the RCE is a practical correction tool, it treats validation nuisance parameters as known and does not account for their estimation uncertainty.

items.title: Measurement Errors in Semiparametric Generalized Regression Models
items.summary: Regression models that ignore measurement error in predictors may produce highly biased estimates leading to erroneous inferences. It is well known that it is extremely difficult to take measurement error into account in Gaussian nonparametric regression. This problem becomes tremendously more difficult when considering other families such as logistic regression, Poisson and negative-binomial. For the first time, we present a method aiming to correct for measurement error when estimating regression functions flexibly covering virtually all distributions and link functions regularly considered in generalized linear models. This approach depends on approximating the first and the second moment of the response after integrating out the true unobserved predictors in a semiparametric generalized linear model. Unlike previous methods, this method is not restricted to truncated splines and can utilize various basis functions. Through extensive simulation studies, we study the performance of our method under many scenarios.

items.title: $K$-Midranks: A robust clustering algorithm for heavy-tailed data with applications to spectroscopy and finance
items.summary: Clustering data with extreme observations and heavy tails can be challenging for methods that rely on distances between raw observations or specific distributional assumptions. We introduce $K$-midranks, a clustering method that replaces observations with coordinatewise ranks and partitions the transformed data using a procedure analogous to $K$-means. This transformation reduces the influence of extreme values while preserving the ordering of observations within each variable. We evaluate $K$-midranks against $K$-means, $K$-medoids, and mixture models based on Gaussian, Student's t, Cauchy, and generalized hyperbolic distributions through simulation studies, and provide some theoretical properties. $K$-midranks generally outperforms the competing methods on Cauchy-shifted data. In contrast, $K$-means and model-based methods perform better on Gaussian data and Student's t data with three degrees of freedom. We demonstrate the method's practical use in grouping samples based on Raman and LIBS spectra and clustering S\&P 500 stocks according to their returns. $K$-midranks achieves competitive performance with model-based methods in the spectroscopy applications and the best performance among the methods considered in the stock-return application. These findings suggest that $K$-midranks provides a useful alternative for clustering data with Cauchy-like heavy tails. An R package implementing the proposed method is available.

items.title: Efficient Prediction of pass@k Scaling in Large Language Models
items.summary: Assessing the capabilities and risks of frontier AI systems is a critical area of research; recent work has shown that repeated sampling can dramatically increase both. For instance, repeated sampling allows models to solve difficult math and coding problems, but it may also increase their risk of being jailbroken. Such results raise a crucial question: how can one accurately predict a model's behavior when scaled to a massive number of attempts, given a vastly smaller sampling budget? This question is directly relevant to model providers, who serve hundreds of millions of users daily, and to governmental regulators, who seek to prevent harms. To answer this question, we make three contributions. First, we find that standard methods for fitting these laws suffer from statistical shortcomings that hinder predictions, especially in data-limited scenarios. Second, we remedy these shortcomings by introducing a robust estimation framework, which uses a beta-binomial distribution to generate more accurate predictions from limited data. Third, we propose a dynamic sampling strategy that allocates a greater budget to harder problems. Combined, these innovations enable more reliable prediction of rare risks and capabilities at a fraction of the computational cost.

items.title: Model-Based Clustering of Longitudinal Functional Data with Hidden Semi-Markov Models
items.summary: Model-based clustering of longitudinal functional data must account both for heterogeneity among curves and for temporal dependence in their latent group memberships. Functional mixture models typically treat curves as exchangeable, while temporal approaches may restrict regime persistence or ignore state-specific functional variation. We propose hidden semi-Markov models for ordered sequences of multivariate functional observations in which each latent regime has a parsimonious, state-specific functional principal subspace, extending functional high-dimensional data clustering (funHDDC) to longitudinal settings. Gaussian, contaminated-Gaussian and multivariate-$t$ emissions accommodate atypical observations, and explicit state-specific sojourn distributions govern regime persistence, with hidden Markov models as the geometric special case. Estimation uses expectation-maximization (EM) and expectation/conditional-maximization (ECM) algorithms with segmental forward-backward recursions, and identifiability is established up to label permutations and spectral indeterminacies. In simulations, temporal dependence yields the largest gains when single curves are weakly informative; with robust emissions, state-specific subspaces outperform a global functional principal component representation; and explicit durations add smaller gains when regimes overlap and sojourns are non-geometric. Applications to air-quality profiles and smartphone activity recordings, evaluated on held-out years and subjects, show improved predictive fit and illustrate how apparent duration effects can reflect time-varying transitions.

items.title: qshap: Fast Shapley Decomposition of $R^2$ for Gradient-Boosted Trees
items.summary: Numerous methods have been developed to quantify feature attributions in individual predictions for tree ensembles. However, many applications require global measures of feature contributions to overall model performance. Although local attribution scores can be aggregated to characterize feature importance, such summaries do not directly decompose measures of predictive performance, such as $R^2$. This article introduces qshap, available in both R and Python, which provides Shapley decomposition of $R^2$ values for gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) to quantify feature-specific contributions to model performance. By decomposing the quadratic loss of individual observations, qshap provides flexible tools to explore the importance of individual features and observations. qshap currently supports widely used GBDT implementations, including xgboost, lightgbm, and catboost, through a unified tree representation and efficient C++ backends. Its modular design can accommodate other GBDT implementations built from binary decision trees. In addition, we introduce a specialized backend for oblivious trees that exploits their symmetric structure to substantially accelerate computation.

items.title: Adaptive Multi-kernel Correntropy Kalman Filter: A Variational Bayesian Approach
items.summary: This paper proposes an adaptive multi-kernel correntropy Kalman filter (AMCKF) for robust state estimation in the presence of heavy-tailed measurement noises and outliers. The multi-kernel correntropy loss is reformulated via half-quadratic (HQ) duality into a quadratic form with auxiliary weights, enabling efficient Kalman-like recursions. We establish a rigorous variational Bayesian framework under the mean-field assumption, deriving closed-form coordinate ascent variational inference updates for joint state and kernel width estimation. To enable online implementation, AMCKF is then proposed as an efficient single-pass approximation of the exact coordinate ascent variational inference (CAVI), where the state and auxiliary variables are updated iteratively via IRLS, followed by a closed-form kernel width update. A forgetting mechanism is designed to prevent over-confidence and ensure long-term adaptability. Simulations on target tracking and IMU attitude estimation demonstrate that the proposed AMCKF significantly outperforms standard KF, VBKF, Student's t-based KF, and fixed-kernel MKCKF in scenarios with sparse outliers, heavy-tailed noise, and mixed disturbances, while maintaining optimal performance under Gaussian conditions.

items.title: Simultaneous Inference for Watermark Proportions in LLM-Generated Text
items.summary: Watermarking enables detection of text generated by large language models, but practical review also requires quantifying retained signals within content of interest. Readers may choose passages based on their content and refine their selections after examining the watermark evidence. We develop simultaneous lower confidence bounds on the fraction of selected tokens that retain a watermark signal. The bounds hold jointly for the full document and any passages selected during review. We develop structure-adaptive closed testing (SACT), which uses a working model of sequential signal clustering to construct scores for calibrated sign-based tests. Under a conditional null model, the bounds have finite-sample simultaneous validity even when the working model is misspecified. An exact reference-family representation recovers the full closed-testing bounds while enabling efficient repeated queries. In a constructed database-recovery review, SACT detects document-wide watermark signals and provides lower confidence bounds on watermark proportions in selected passages. Assessing related passages together gives a sharper lower bound on their combined signal count. In simulations spanning two watermarking mechanisms and a range of signal strengths and densities, SACT generally has higher power than competing methods.

items.title: Partial Identification under Imperfect Compliance via Cross-World Correlation Restriction
items.summary: This article develops a unified partial identification approach for the average treatment effect (ATE) and the local average treatment effect (LATE) in randomized experiments with imperfect compliance, incorporating the cross-world correlation between potential treatment statuses. Even under random assignment and exclusion restriction, the correlation is unidentified. However, given the two identified marginals, it uniquely determines the relative proportions of the four principal strata, with monotonicity corresponding to a special case. We derive explicit sharp bounds for both the ATE and LATE at a fixed correlation and extend the results to prespecified correlation ranges, providing a sensitivity analysis that incorporates substantive information about compliance behavior. For the ATE, the lower bound decreases and the upper bound increases with the correlation. Although imposing monotonicity does not tighten the conventional Balke--Pearl bounds, we show that restricting the correlation can yield tighter bounds, even when defiers remain possible. For the LATE, the sharp bounds may not vary monotonically with the correlation, and we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for point identification of the LATE at any feasible correlation value, with the conventional Wald ratio identification result under monotonicity as a special case. In addition, we derive a breakdown point for the correlation that determines when the Wald ratio falls outside the sharp identified set for the LATE. Applications to four empirical studies illustrate how cross-world correlation restrictions tighten the sharp bounds for the ATE and LATE and assess the breakdown of the Wald ratio.

items.title: Deriving Complete Constraints in Hidden Variable Models
items.summary: Hidden variable graphical models can sometimes imply constraints on the observable distribution that are more complex than simple conditional independence relations. These observable constraints can falsify assumptions of the model and can be used to constrain estimation procedures to improve statistical efficiency. Knowing the complete set of observable constraints is thus ideal, but this can be difficult to determine in many settings. In models with categorical observed variables and a joint distribution that is completely characterized by linear relations to the probabilities of unobservable response function variables, we develop a systematic method for deriving the complete set of observable constraints. We illustrate the method in several settings, including ones that imply both inequality and equality constraints.

items.title: Weak instrumental variables due to ignored nonlinearities in panel data: An Orthogonal Super Learner Control Function estimator
items.summary: A triangular structural panel data model with additively separable individual-specific effects is used to model the causal effect of a covariate on an outcome variable when there are unobservable confounders with some of them time-invariant. In this setup, a linear specification for the reduced-form equation might be problematic when the conditional mean of the endogenous covariate and the instrumental variables is nonlinear in the population. The reason is that ignoring the nonlinearity could lead to weak instruments (instruments are weakly correlated with the endogenous covariate) due to misspecification as shown using a generalized concentration parameter for panel data. As a solution, we propose a triangular simultaneous equation model for panel data with additive separable individual-specific fixed effects composed of a linear structural equation with a nonlinear reduced form equation. The parameter of interest is the structural parameter of the endogenous variable. The identification of this parameter is obtained under the assumption of available exclusion restrictions and using a control function approach. We derive a Neyman orthogonal score, and we provide an estimator that we call Orthogonal Super Learner Control Function (Orthogonal SLCF) estimator. The estimation procedure is composed of two main steps and cross-fitting. First, we estimate the control function using a super learner. In the following step, we use the estimated control function to control for endogeneity in the structural equation. Cross-fitting is done across the individual dimension. The estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal achieving a parametric rate of convergence. We show that the Orthogonal SLCF estimator is equivalent to the plug-in IV estimator but not equivalent to the naive plug-in 2SLS estimator which is not root-NT consistent.

items.title: Cross-Order Information-Guided Estimation for Non-Uniform Hypergraphs
items.summary: Many real-world interactions involve groups of nodes rather than pairs. A non-uniform hypergraph records such interactions as hyperedges of different orders, where the order counts the nodes in a hyperedge. Full estimation evaluates every candidate hyperedge, whose number grows exponentially with the order, and classical remedies sacrifice higher-order information or aggravate computation. The orders are not isolated: the lower orders, cheap to compute and rich in information, reveal where higher-order hyperedges are likely to occur. We propose CINE (Cross-order Information-guided Negative-sampling Estimation) under a latent space model in which all orders share latent positions. Starting from order two, CINE climbs one order at a time. At each higher order, CINE keeps all present hyperedges, samples a small subset of negative examples guided by lower-order scores, and corrects for the known inclusion probabilities to preserve the target of full estimation. CINE thereby lets users choose the trade-off between computation time and estimation accuracy: the retained orders and the sampling budget set the time, and the retained information provably approaches full-data information as the sampling budget grows. In simulations, CINE approaches the accuracy of full estimation at a small fraction of its computation time, and larger teams in MADStat reveal research associations.

items.title: Within-task hazards of AI agents: unidentified by time-horizon curves, identified by repeated runs
items.summary: The time horizon of an AI agent is read off a curve: the probability that the agent completes a task, plotted against the time a human needs for it. Several recent analyses fit survival models to this curve and conclude that agents' hazard of failure declines as a task goes on. The curve cannot support that conclusion. Every log-logistic horizon curve with slope $β\le1$ is a mixture of constant-hazard curves, and in a proportional-hazards frailty model the same curve is produced by every within-task Weibull shape $k\geβ$. If runs of a task are conditionally independent, repeated runs restore identification within this model: the probability that two runs both succeed is the single-run curve shifted by $1/k$ on the $\log_2$ time axis. Without the Weibull form, the horizontal distance between these two curves still bears on the direction of the hazard: if the average within-task hazard is non-increasing, the distance is at least one, and so is the population limit of a two-step estimator when the cross-section is log-logistic. We decompose the bias of that estimator into a violation of the shift and a first-step misspecification term, and examine five mechanisms that can break the shift. On METR's public run-level data, under stated assumptions that the data cannot verify, no model's 95% interval for $1/k$ lies entirely above one, and for the five frontier models in the TH1.0 release every interval from runs in different batches lies below one. Under the same assumptions, taken interval by interval and given a log-logistic cross-section, these intervals reject a non-increasing average hazard for the five models, whereas in TH1.1 the result depends on how human times were obtained. Whether $k>1$ reflects a hazard that rises within a task or tasks whose difficulty human time measures only loosely needs experiments that observe the same task at several lengths.

items.title: Beyond Point Forecasts: A Survey on Probabilistic Forecasting for Time Series and Spatiotemporal Data
items.summary: Probabilistic forecasting is central to decision-making under uncertainty, yet its methodological landscape has become increasingly fragmented across temporal and spatiotemporal forecasting, statistical modeling, machine learning, and deep generative modeling. This survey develops a unified perspective by organizing probabilistic forecasting methods according to where and how uncertainty is introduced into the forecasting pipeline. Our taxonomy connects model-agnostic approaches including ensembles and distribution-free calibration, with model-intrinsic approaches spanning Bayesian modeling, parametric predictive distributions, distributional regression, and modern generative models, and further examines the emerging role of time series foundation models. Beyond methodological synthesis, we identify the assumptions, computational demands, and forms of uncertainty represented by different paradigms, and translate these distinctions into data-driven and domain-specific guidance for method selection. We complement the survey with a cross-paradigm empirical study on univariate, multivariate, and spatiotemporal forecasting tasks. The results reveal that no single uncertainty-quantification paradigm dominates across settings. Calibration, sharpness, predictive accuracy, and computational efficiency can lead to substantially different model preferences, while expressive generative models and zero-shot foundation models exhibit markedly different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. Lastly, we identify unresolved challenges surrounding uncertainty in evolving dependency structures, physics-informed predictive distributions, forecasting extreme events, handling count-valued, directional, and continuous-time series, and the development of unified software resources. Our survey provides both a conceptual framework and a practical roadmap for probabilistic forecasting research.

items.title: Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoders for Scalable Phenotyping of Health Trajectories
items.summary: Clustering longitudinal health trajectories requires handling high-dimensional measurements, irregular visit times, and subject-level heterogeneity while retaining clinically interpretable structure. Existing methods address this only partially: latent-class mixed models yield an interpretable, covariate-driven partition but do not scale past a handful of markers, while deep time-series clustering scales at the cost of that structure and generally requires a common time grid. We introduce the Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoder (LCMM-VAE), a deep generative model whose latent prior is a mixture of class-specific linear mixed models, so that each subject's latent trajectory decomposes into its class mean trajectory and a subject-specific deviation. We derive a variational EM algorithm whose class responsibilities, random effects and mixed-model parameters are updated in closed form, and provide identifiability guarantees under stated conditions. Experiments on simulated and real longitudinal cohorts show that LCMM-VAE returns a partition, a reconstruction of incomplete trajectories and interpretable class-level dynamics at once, while remaining competitive with classical and deep baselines.

items.title: From the ELBO to Maximum Likelihood: Convergence of Variational Autoencoders for Nonlinear Mixed-Effects Modeling
items.summary: Nonlinear mixed-effects (NLME) models are the central statistical models of pharmacometrics, where they support dose selection, individualized dosing and regulatory decisions in drug development. Statistically, NLME modeling is a marginalized likelihood problem. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) solve such problems with a neural network encoder that amortizes the approximation of the intractable posterior distribution, and allow the integration of AI components into NLME modeling. This paper provides the convergence analysis of the VAE-NLME algorithm. First, its version for the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is proven to converge almost surely to the set of stationary points of the ELBO, without assuming that the encoder is trained exactly. Second, the final VAE-NLME algorithm trains the encoder on the ELBO by gradient-based optimization and uses it as proposal for importance-weighted sufficient statistics. It converges almost surely to the set of stationary points of the marginal log-likelihood, without any assumption on the training of the encoder. Thus, it combines the fast gradient-based training of VAEs with the limit of maximum likelihood estimation.

items.title: Functional Characterization of Choice-Implied Subjective Time in Intertemporal Financial Decisions
items.summary: Intertemporal choice is usually summarized by a discount rate or a predefined parametric discount function, leaving differences in the shape of individual discounting over the horizon unobserved. This paper proposes a Functional Data Analysis framework that reconstructs, for each respondent, a choice-implied subjective-time trajectory $τ_i(t)$ from monetary equivalence judgments collected at thirteen horizons between seven days and five years. Equivalence judgments are mapped into discount factors, regularized by monotone shape-constrained smoothing, and converted into trajectories under the representation $f_i(t)=\exp\{-k_iτ_i(t)\}$, with $k_i$ an operational scale. The trajectories are analyzed through derivatives, functional principal component analysis and clustering of the component scores, compared with exponential, Weber-Fechner and Stevens benchmarks in sample and in a leave-one-horizon-out design, and related to an explicit subjective-time positioning task. A Monte Carlo study evaluates the recovery of trajectory shape and group structure. The empirical application uses an online multilingual survey with 141 respondents; 140 are eligible, 61 report the full future amount at every horizon and 19 provide profiles that do not determine a decreasing discount curve, leaving 60 identified trajectories. The mean trajectory is predominantly concave, two functional components account for 92.0% of the variability of the centered trajectories, and four profiles that differ in when subjective time accumulates relative to the mean are identified; the profiles also differ in discounting intensity. Parametric subjective-time models are competitive in predicting held-out judgments, while partitions based on their parameters do not reproduce the functional partition. No statistically detectable correspondence with the explicit positioning task is found.

items.title: Exponential Smoothing for Time Series of Random Objects
items.summary: Time series of random objects, such as covariance matrices, probability distributions, and functional data, call for forecasting methods that do not rely on arithmetic operations. We introduce geodesic exponential smoothing for time series in Hadamard spaces. The forecast level moves a fixed fraction of the way along the geodesic towards each new observation. The smoothing parameter is estimated by minimising the average squared distance between observations and forecasts. The method involves a single scalar parameter, assumes no stationarity, and updates online in constant time per observation. We further introduce an innovations mechanism under which each observation has conditional Fréchet mean equal to the current level, the metric-space analogue of the innovations state-space model. We show via the quasilinearisation of Hadamard spaces that the level is a martingale in a nonlinear sense, that the spread of the data from the initial state grows at least linearly in time, and that their quasi-autocorrelation at any fixed lag tends to one. We prove almost-sure consistency and asymptotic normality of the smoothing-parameter estimator. Three real-data applications, spanning covariance-matrix, distributional, and functional time series, assess the forecasting performance against structurally heavier alternatives.

items.title: Breaking Resonance: Square-root acceleration for Metropolis-adjusted randomized Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
items.summary: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with a fixed integration time can fail to mix because of resonances, and randomizing the integration time removes them. We prove that Metropolis-adjusted HMC with velocity Verlet and random integration times mixes from a warm start in a number of transitions that does not depend on the condition number, for every integration-time law satisfying a Fourier condition that we call non-resonant; uniform, exponential and triangular laws are examples. For a target density proportional to $e^{-U}$ on $\mathbb R^d$, where $U$ is $m$-strongly convex with $L$-Lipschitz gradient and $L_H$-Lipschitz Hessian and $κ=L/m$, the number of gradient evaluations needed to reach a fixed total variation accuracy is, up to constants and logarithmic factors, $\sqrt{κd}+\sqrt{L_H}\,(d/m)^{3/4}$. This is the first square-root condition-number bound for this sampler beyond Gaussian targets. The proof converts relative-entropy contraction of the unadjusted proposal into a conductance bound for the adjusted chain, and shows that the integration-time law enters only through its characteristic function. Hessian regularity cannot be dropped for a fixed step size: without it there are targets in the class for which the cost is at least of order $κ^{2/3}$, up to logarithmic factors, even from a warm start.

items.title: Anytime-valid goodness-of-fit test by $e$-spacings
items.summary: To perform an anytime-valid goodness-of-fit test, we propose spacing-based $e$-processes that control the type-I error rate under arbitrary stopping rules. Based on the maximum spacing of order statistics, we construct spacing-based $e$-processes for nonparametrically testing distribution. The resulting procedures are simple and computationally efficient, and are power-consistent. We call them $e$-spacing tests. This approach is especially powerful in detecting localized discrepancy between the data-generating density and the null density. Under mild conditions, the logarithm of the proposed $e$-process is asymptotically equivalent to that of the oracle-optimal $e$-process. We further generalize the construction from maximal spacing to maximum spacing set in the form of the $1/k$ fraction of the largest $m$th order spacings, as a measure of the lower-level set of density. It boosts power under more global discrepancy from the null. Furthermore, we propose a greedy predictable scheme, via argmax or softmax rules, to combine multiple $e$-spacing testing strategies. We prove that it optimally tunes the $e$-spacing test. The proposed approach is readily generalizable to multivariate testing via a coordinate-wise Rosenblatt-transform. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed methods perform favorably relative to the considered anytime-valid competitors as well as various types of multiple test-adjusted Kolmogorov--Smirnov tests.

items.title: Seldon TFM family: Seldon-Mini, Seldon and Seldon+
items.summary: We introduce Seldon, a family of tabular foundation models. Our classifier Seldon+ ranks first among 15 models on TabBench, our benchmark of 124 classification datasets, and on its variant with missing values. In our own runs of public benchmarks, it also ranks first on BeyondArena IID classification and TabBench-Bio, and second on TabArena classification. The open-weight models Seldon-Mini (27M parameters) and Seldon (213M parameters) both lie on the TabArena Pareto front of Elo against inference time: no entry is both more accurate and faster. On TabArena, Seldon ranks fourth and Seldon-Mini seventh among 109 leaderboard entries, and on the IID track of BeyondArena, Seldon ranks second among 42 entries. Seldon-Mini and Seldon handle both classification and regression, use an architecture similar to those of Kumo-Tabular, TabFM and TabPFN-3.5, and are trained on synthetic tables only.

items.title: On Approximate Computation of Critical Points
items.summary: We show that computing even coarse approximations of critical points is intractable for simple classes of nonconvex functions. We first present a family of $n$-variate cubic polynomials with coefficients in $\{-1,0,1\}$ that have exact critical points but for which no polynomial-time algorithm can write down a $\sqrt{n}/4$-approximate critical point in its standard representation. We then show that computational hardness persists when an exact critical point has a short representation. More specifically, we prove that for every fixed $η>0$, unless P $=$ NP, no polynomial-time (or even pseudo-polynomial-time) algorithm can take an $n$-variate cubic polynomial with rational coefficients ${c_α}$ and return a point with gradient norm at most $(\max_α|c_α|)n^{1/2-η}$ whenever the polynomial has a critical point in $\{-1,0,1\}^n$. The algorithm may return an arbitrary point on all other inputs. Both results are essentially tight in their dependence on the dimension $n$. We also prove hardness results for lower-bounded functions and for an alternative notion of approximation, in which approximation is measured by distance to an exact critical point. Overall, our results stand in contrast to the commonly held belief that, in nonconvex optimization, approximate computation of critical points is a tractable task.

items.title: Unbiased Approximate Vector-Jacobian Products for Efficient Backpropagation
items.summary: In this work we introduce methods to reduce the computational and memory costs of training deep neural networks. Our approach consists in replacing exact vector-jacobian products by randomized, unbiased approximations thereof during backpropagation. We provide a theoretical analysis of the trade-off between the number of epochs needed to achieve a target precision and the cost reduction for each epoch. We then identify specific unbiased estimates of vector-jacobian products for which we establish desirable optimality properties of minimal variance under sparsity constraints. Finally we provide in-depth experiments on multi-layer perceptrons, BagNets and Visual Transfomers architectures. These validate our theoretical results, and confirm the potential of our proposed unbiased randomized backpropagation approach for reducing the cost of deep learning.

items.title: Asymptotically Efficient Conformal Inference for Individual Treatment Effects under Multivalued Treatments
items.summary: Most existing conformal inference methods for individual treatment effects are limited to settings with binary treatments. For multiple treatments, propensity score-derived weights often suffer from statistical instability, while contiguous prediction intervals may span low-density regions between modes of potential outcome distributions, leading to inefficient prediction sets. We propose adaptive prediction sets for counterfactual outcomes under multivalued treatments by combining KuLSIF-based density ratio estimation with highest predictive density (HPD) conformal scores derived from conditional density estimates. Both estimators share a reproducing kernel Hilbert space least-squares formulation, which simplifies theoretical derivation and analysis. The resulting prediction sets are robust to heteroscedasticity and multimodal outcome distributions and effectively eliminate low-density regions between distribution modes. Under unconfoundedness assumption and regularity conditions, we prove that the proposed method converges to optimal HPD sets under covariate shift and establish its asymptotic conditional validity and statistical efficiency.
