By jointly inferring calibration parameters and model discrepancies within a Bayesian framework, our model recovers more physically meaningful parameters and provides reliable uncertainty quantification. Crucially, this accurate parameter recovery enables reliable extrapolative prediction, a challenge current methods largely fail to address. We validate the approach through numerical studies and a real-world industrial application: predicting the thermal stability of multilayer mirrors in extreme ultraviolet lithography. In this application, our method accurately predicts high-temperature responses far beyond the training domain, significantly outperforming existing calibration methods.

items.title: Gated Payoff-Weighted Net Profit Maximization For Online Portfolio Selection With Transaction Costs
items.summary: In this paper, we study online portfolio selection (OLPS) problems. The net profit maximization (NPM) acting upon Adaptive Online Moving Average (AOLMA), namely the AOLNPM strategy in portfolio selection, trades when forecast gain exceeds the transaction cost. In essence, this method relies heavily on calibrated forecasts. Indeed, we show that AOLMA forecasts overstate the realized relative returns. We therefore design a gate that adjusts how strongly an AOLMA forecast is used; for each asset, it learns the recent mixture proportion assigned to AOLMA from predictive likelihoods against a neutral forecast (no change). The proportion therefore estimates the extent to which the forecast is realized. We then feed the resulting forecast into the NPM portfolio rule, where the gate acts as an asset-specific cost threshold. A payoff-weighted fund combines gated NPM experts with fixed decay factors in proportion to their wealth and needs no learning rate. On nine datasets with a transaction cost rate of 0.1%, our method produces 5.9 times the wealth of AOLNPM in geometric mean and sits above AOLNPM on every dataset, with its preponderance growing with the cost rate.

items.title: Handling Missing Data in Probabilistic Regression Trees
items.summary: Probabilistic regression trees are a smooth alternative to classical regression trees, consistent in the complete-data case, producing continuous predictions through probabilistic split assignments. This paper extends this framework by proposing three approaches to accommodate missing predictor values directly during tree construction, without a separate imputation step. These modifications are defined to preserve the fundamental probabilistic properties of the original methodology, including probability conservation and marginal compatibility, under arbitrary patterns of missing covariate values. The proposed methods are evaluated on several real-world datasets exhibiting different levels of missingness and are compared with classical regression trees. In addition, a semi-synthetic study, in which missing values are injected completely at random, at random and not at random, compares the proposed strategies with impute-then-fit pipelines based on commonly applied imputation methods.

items.title: Exact, narrow and fast: Use the Gaffke confidence interval for the mean of a discrete bounded variable
items.summary: Survey ratings, test scores and many other data take a few known values, and we often want a confidence interval for their mean. For small samples, or for means close to the smallest or largest value, the usual intervals cover the true mean much less often than they claim. The interval of Gaffke generalizes the Clopper-Pearson interval to any finite set of values, and a recent proof of Gaffke's conjecture shows that its coverage is at least the nominal level for every sample size and every distribution. Its endpoints, however, are quantiles of a weighted sum of Dirichlet variables, with no closed form. This note makes three contributions. First, a fast and accurate algorithm for the endpoints: a Fourier inversion integral on a line through the saddle point gives tail probabilities with a small relative error, a Gauss-Legendre rule on geometric panels converges at the same rate wherever the singularities are, and a Newton iteration needs 2.6 evaluations per endpoint on average. The cost is $O(kN)$ operations for $k$ values and $N$ quadrature nodes, and $N$ does not grow with the sample size, so an interval takes less than a millisecond for any $n$. Second, an experimental comparison with the published intervals: for $n \le 30$, the Gaffke interval is the shortest of the intervals that keep the level, 17 to 20% shorter than the betting interval of Waudby-Smith and Ramdas and 19 to 37% shorter than Anderson's, while the shorter intervals (Wald, Student, profile likelihood, Bayesian) cover the mean less than 50% of the time for some distributions. Third, tested Python and R packages and a web page, with endpoints accurate to $10^{-12}$ of the range of the values. So the interval is exact, narrow and fast, and we recommend it.

items.title: GeoFusion: An Uncertain Machine Learning Framework for Sensor Fusion
items.summary: High positioning precision is a critical requirement in many Global Positioning System (GPS) applications, yet achieving it with affordable smartphone sensors remains an open challenge. Existing approaches treat each GPS observation as an absolute point, discarding the uncertainty inherent in the measurement conditions and leaving the cooperative potential of multiple phones observing the same location untapped. In this work, we propose GeoFusion, a three-stage uncertain machine learning framework for cooperative sensor fusion. In the first stage, each GPS observation is modeled as an uncertain object using one of two proposed models: the volcano function, grounded in satellite geometry, and the empirically derived mountain function, built from the statistical structure of real smartphone data. In the second stage, uncertain objects are clustered by location event using partitional and graph-based algorithms. In the third stage, the cluster output is refined using filter-based and learning-based estimators. Experiments on the Google Smartphone Decimeter Challenge dataset show that uncertainty modeling is a primary driver of precision gains: the mountain function significantly outperforms the geometry-only volcano function, and uncertainty-aware UK-medoids significantly outperforms its certain counterpart, k-medoids. A post-clustering deep neural network further refines the cluster estimates, and the recommended configuration achieves a mean absolute error of 2.90 +/- 0.15 meters on held-out test drives, comparable to and on average below the best reported single-phone precision of approximately 3 meters, demonstrating the potential of cooperative uncertainty-aware fusion for affordable GPS sensors.

items.title: A Single-Loop Method with Optimal Leading-Order Oracle Complexity for Optimization and Game Stationarity in Nonconvex--Concave Minimax Optimization
items.summary: We develop a single-loop first-order framework for smooth nonconvex--concave minimax optimization, with matching leading-order upper and lower bounds for optimization and game stationarity in a projected zero-respecting oracle model. We propose a single-loop projected damped extragradient method coupling projected extragradient updates with dual momentum and a moving proximal center. Each iteration uses at most three gradient evaluations, without nested subproblems. For game stationarity, a deterministic best iterate has first-order residual below $\varepsilon$ with leading oracle complexity $\mathcal{O}(L^{3/2}D_Y^{1/2}Δ_φ\varepsilon^{-5/2})$, where $L$ is the gradient Lipschitz constant, $D_Y$ bounds the dual feasible-set diameter, and $Δ_φ$ is the initial-point-dependent value-function gap. For optimization stationarity, a uniformly selected iterate has expected squared Moreau-envelope gradient norm at most $\varepsilon^2$ with leading oracle complexity $\mathcal{O}(L^2D_YΔ_φ\varepsilon^{-3})$. Matching lower bounds are $Ω(L^{3/2}D_Y^{1/2}Δ_φ\varepsilon^{-5/2})$ for game stationarity and $Ω(L^2D_YΔ_φ\varepsilon^{-3})$ for optimization stationarity over projected zero-respecting first-order methods. Under dual strong concavity, the same framework achieves leading first-order oracle complexity $\mathcal{O}(\sqrtκLΔ_φ\varepsilon^{-2})$ under both criteria, where $κ$ is the dual condition number. Matching lower bounds hold for both criteria in the same oracle model. To our knowledge, this is the first work to close the oracle complexity gap for smooth nonconvex--concave minimax optimization under both stationarity criteria by simultaneously improving upper and lower bounds in the projected zero-respecting oracle model.

items.title: Logistic Credibility with Temporal Decay: Extending Bühlmann--Straub for Commercial Lines
items.summary: Bühlmann--Straub (B-S) credibility blends an account's own experience with a complement (the benchmark rate) using the weight Z = E/(E+K), where E is exposure and K is a constant estimated from the portfolio. It assumes the same K for every account, equal influence for recent and older years, and a fixed complement. On held-out US Commercial Auto data the constant-K assumption fails for small accounts: standard B-S gives them a calibration slope of 4.0 (ideal 1.0; 90% bootstrap CI 2.5--4.9), i.e. they are under-credited. We propose a joint framework that relaxes all three assumptions while keeping an interpretable credibility weight: Z is a logistic function of observable account characteristics, older experience is down-weighted by an exponentially weighted moving average with an estimated decay rate, and weight, decay rate and complement are fitted in one likelihood. Rolling B-S is a special case, so extensions can be tested by likelihood-ratio test. On 96 companies with the last two accident years held out, the proposed model brings the small-account slope from 4.0 to 1.0 and reduces exposure-weighted prediction error by 25% relative to standard B-S (90% bootstrap interval 7%--42%). A step-by-step patched B-S comes within 2.5% overall but deteriorates for small accounts when recency weighting is added. A mixed-effects benchmark, which shrinks almost exactly as B-S does, is outperformed overall; it does better for mid-sized accounts in the test period (not statistically significant) but miscalibrates small ones. The decay rate falls with account size (0.60, 0.84 and 0.13 for Small, Mid and Large), so large accounts rely mainly on recent experience; Other Liability and a simulation study support the mechanisms. The model needs only account-year summaries and gives underwriters a credibility weight, complement and renewal rate.

items.title: Pharmacy stock and post-earthquake access to medicines in Tokyo: modeling choices that change recovery judgments
items.summary: Community pharmacies sustain access to medicines after an earthquake only while open, staffed and stocked. Accessibility models rarely represent stock depletion, and the assumptions this requires may change conclusions about recovery. We examine these assumptions for over-the-counter (OTC) medicines supplied by 4,748 registered pharmacies in Tokyo's 23 wards during the first week after a magnitude-7.3 scenario earthquake. A two-step floating catchment area model computes walking accessibility for 2,651 grid cells (500 m) under 10,000 sampled combinations of stock duration, staffing, operation and demand. Results are expressed as Retention: post-disaster accessibility divided by the same cell's pre-disaster accessibility. First, the assumed link between stock and service, the supply a pharmacy can still provide, determines the recovery verdict. If service falls in proportion to remaining stock, mean Retention declines from 0.479 (days 2-3) to 0.273 (days 4-7). If service is maintained until stock falls below one quarter, the mean rises instead, although low-end (10th-percentile) outcomes still decline. Measuring at the start of each period rather than averaging over it also reverses the trend. Second, a simple model that rescales a fixed map by citywide supply and demand reproduces citywide patterns but cannot evaluate where pharmacies close or where capacity is added; a spatial model run once on average inputs can. Third, four floating catchment methods agree on overall rankings (rank correlation 0.81), but their lowest-ranked 10% of cells overlap only partially (Jaccard index 0.56). Disaster assessments should report stock assumptions and low-end outcomes, and treat local priority areas as method-dependent.

items.title: More Bang for the Buck: Improving the Inference of Large Language Models at a Fixed Budget using Reset and Discard (ReD)
items.summary: The performance of large language models (LLMs) on verifiable tasks is usually measured by pass@k, the probability of solving a problem correctly at least once in k trials. At a fixed budget, a more suitable metric is coverage@cost, the average number of unique problems solved as a function of the total number of attempts. We connect the two metrics and show that the empirically-observed power-law behavior in pass@k leads to a sublinear growth of the coverage@cost (diminishing returns). To solve this problem, we propose Reset-and-Discard (ReD), a query method of LLMs that increases coverage@cost for a given budget, regardless of the pass@k form. Moreover, given a pass@k, we can quantitatively predict the savings in the total number of attempts using ReD. If pass@k is not available for the model, ReD can infer its power-law exponent. Experiments across coding (HumanEval), math (GSM8K), and reasoning (MMLU-Pro) benchmarks, as well as real GitHub issues solved by a coding agent (SWE-bench Lite), demonstrate that ReD substantially reduces the required attempts, tokens, and USD cost to reach a desired coverage, while also offering an efficient way to measure inference power-laws. ReD's advantage is maintained for imperfect verifiers.

items.title: Probabilities for asymmetric p-outside values
items.summary: In 2017-2020 Jordanova and co-authors investigate probabilities for p-outside values and determine them in many particular cases. They show that these probabilities are closely related to the concept for heavy tails. Tukey's boxplots are very popular and useful in practice. Analogously to the chi-square-criterion, the relative frequencies of the events an observation to fall in different their parts, compared with the corresponding probabilities an observation of a fixed probability distribution to fall in the same parts, help the practitioners to find the accurate probability distribution of the observed random variable. These open the door to work with the distribution sensitive estimators which in many cases are more accurate, especially for small sample investigations. All these methods, however, suffer from the disadvantage that they use inter quantile range in a symmetric way. The concept for outside values should take into account the form of the distribution. Therefore, here, we give possibility for more asymmetry in analysis of the tails of the distributions. We suggest new theoretical and empirical box-plots and characteristics of the tails of the distributions. These are theoretical asymmetric p-outside values functions. We partially investigate some of their properties and give some examples. It turns out that they do not depend on the center and the scaling factor of the distribution. Therefore, they are very appropriate for comparison of the tails of the distribution, and later on, for estimation of the parameters, which govern the tail behaviour of the cumulative distribution function.

items.title: Does Increasing Government Spending on Tertiary Education Provide a Return on Investment? A Bayesian Causal Inference Analysis
items.summary: Does public spending on tertiary (university) education generate a positive fiscal return once general economic growth is separated out? Cross-country data make this hard to answer because growing economies naturally collect more tax, international ratios divide per-student spending by GDP per person and student headcount, and cohorts take years to graduate. We assemble a five-year panel of 121 countries (1985-2024) and fit continuous-treatment Multivariate Bayesian Causal Forests modelling four tax changes jointly whilst adjusting for starting conditions, predicted funding, and follow-up growth. A +10 percentage-point (pp) increase in per-student spending (% of GDP per person) shifts the tax mix toward direct income and profit taxation by +0.36 pp after 5 years (P = 0.93, posterior probability of a positive effect) and +0.71 pp after 10 years (P = 0.96). Overall tax-to-GDP takes a decade to respond: 10-year total non-resource tax rises by +0.24 pp of GDP (P = 0.89; +0.31 pp, P = 0.94 across four chains, retaining the conservative single-chain baseline) and direct income tax by +0.12 pp (P = 0.90; +0.15 pp, P = 0.93 across four chains) per +10 pp of per-student spending, by +0.37 pp (P > 0.99) after five-year within-country increases, and by +0.22 pp in total tax (P = 0.95) and +0.15 pp in direct income tax (P = 0.98) per +25% increase in real PPP dollars per student. Comparing one cohort's degree cost against its 40-year career taxes shows a typical three- to five-fold expected total tax return in high-income economies with wide intervals reflecting macro noise (EUR 2.4B in Ireland returning EUR 9.7B in total tax, 95% CI EUR -10B to +32B, net-profit probability 0.77, and EUR 2.9B in direct income tax; EUR 11.6B in the UK returning EUR 58B, 95% CI EUR -60B to +190B), whereas expanding the budget without protecting spending per student yields no return.

items.title: Optimal Labelling Designs for Sequential Decisions on Language Model Updates
items.summary: When a large language model (LLM) is updated, its developer must decide whether accuracy improved, worsened or stayed within a tolerance. An LLM judge can assess every prompt cheaply but imperfectly, while human labels are costly. We propose Sequential Decisions with Optimal Labelling Designs (SOLD), which labels one prompt at a time, uses the judge to correct the estimate of the change in accuracy and to choose the prompts, and stops once the evidence is conclusive. A wrong decision has probability at most a prespecified level whenever labelling stops. The commonly used Neyman allocation minimises the variance of the estimate and therefore rarely labels prompts that the judge is confident about. It can need far more draws when the outcomes of these prompts could still fall far below the judge's prediction. We instead derive the design that gathers evidence fastest, which labels each prompt with probability at least proportional to how far its outcome could fall below the prediction. As the level tends to zero, no procedure based on the judge-corrected estimates needs fewer draws than SOLD. In simulations and on the EVOUNA and MMLU-Pro datasets, SOLD needed fewer labels than the other methods.

items.title: Checking the Cumulative Exposure Model: Cumulative Chi-Squared Goodness-of-Fit Tests for Interval-Monitored Step-Stress Life Tests
items.summary: In an interval-monitored step-stress life test the data are the numbers of devices that fail between consecutive inspections. These cells are ordered in time, but the usual goodness-of-fit check, Pearson's statistic, ignores the order. We propose goodness-of-fit tests based on the cumulative residuals, the differences between the empirical and the fitted distribution functions at the inspection times, with the parameters estimated by the minimum density power divergence estimator. The two statistics are Taguchi's cumulative chi-squared statistic and its version with constant weights, the classical members of a family of cumulative divergences for ordered categories, with the null probabilities replaced by those of the fitted model. For the exponential cumulative exposure model with a log-linear link we prove the existence, uniqueness and consistency of the estimator under explicit conditions, and we derive the limit distribution of the statistics under the null hypothesis and under contiguous alternatives: a weighted chi-square distribution with $L-s$ terms, where $L$ is the number of inspection times and $s$ the number of parameters. The critical values are obtained by plugging the estimated weights into Imhof's formula, and the procedure has asymptotic size $α$. A local-power analysis and a simulation study show that the cumulative statistics are more powerful than Pearson's statistic against a wrong lifetime distribution, and that the limit distribution is accurate already with $50$ devices. An application to light bulbs tested under step voltage illustrates the method.

items.title: Conformal Selection under Prevalence Shift: FDR Bounds and Finite Calibration
items.summary: Conformalized Benjamini--Hochberg (cfBH) uses labeled calibration data to select candidates while controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) under suitable assumptions. We examine how differences between source and test populations affect FDR and power. When non-target scores have the same distribution in both populations, existing results guarantee FDR control for clipped cfBH if non-targets are at least as common in the source population as in the test population. When this prevalence condition fails, FDR can exceed the nominal level. We determine the worst-case FDR in large samples. For example, a nominal level of 10\% can yield FDR approaching 40\% when the source population has 20\% non-targets and the test population has 80\%. Calibrating only against labeled non-targets avoids this restriction on their proportions, provided their score distributions still agree. However, every nonempty selection must contain a minimum number of candidates. This requirement can limit power when few true targets are present. More calibration non-targets can lower the minimum. We use the same minimum to bound FDR inflation when non-target score distributions differ. In worst-case examples, a contamination fraction inversely proportional to the number of calibration non-targets can drive FDR close to 100\% in large test pools. A random labeled sample from the test population provides a representative calibration reference. Pooling its non-targets with source non-targets can improve power when their score distributions agree. Without this agreement, we give a correction for pooling that controls FDR but selects only a subset of the candidates selected using the random sample alone. Simulations and molecular-screening experiments on AqSolDB, with no shared molecular identities across data splits, illustrate these findings.

items.title: Community Detection in Fuzzy Social Networks through Fuzzy Co-Membership Relations over Alpha-Cut Realizations
items.summary: In fuzzy social networks the ties between actors are triangular fuzzy numbers, and community detection applied to their cores ignores how the partition depends on their vagueness. We propose a fuzzy co-membership relation obtained by running the Louvain algorithm on crisp networks compatible with the alpha-cuts of the ties and integrating the proportions of co-assignment over alpha. The relation is positive semidefinite; from it we derive a consensus partition, the number of groups, membership degrees and an assignment ambiguity index. In simulations from stochastic block models the relation does not yield better partitions than symmetric perturbations of the cores of the same size. Its ambiguity index is more closely associated with the structural position of the actors and identifies actors split between two groups when the vagueness is concentrated on them; when the asymmetry of the fuzzy ties points towards the latent tie strength, its co-membership degrees have a lower Brier score. The interval-weighted Louvain algorithm estimates the number of communities more accurately. In two departmental collaboration networks the observed ambiguity is lower than under permuted ratings, while the partitions depend on the symmetrization of directed ratings and on the coding of non-response.

items.title: FAER: A Negative-Result Audit of Offline Trajectory Replay Selection on GSM8K
items.summary: Offline trajectory replay selects model-generated reasoning traces from a frozen cache for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), yet cache-side answer correctness need not predict downstream accuracy on unseen problems. We report a failure-retaining audit of offline response SFT on GSM8K with Qwen3-1.7B fp16 LoRA over a frozen 384-row cache (256 training rows and 128 excluded held-out rows). Across three seeds (13, 17, 23) on a 256-problem test split, all three 32-row replay rules (uniform, format-feedback, and feedback-aware) obtain mean strict accuracies (0.7786, 0.7682, and 0.7956) below the no-update base model (0.8008), and every paired 95% confidence interval spans zero. Selector ranking is post-hoc unidentified (3 completed selectors versus the repaired protocol's minimum of 5, with rank correlation spanning both signs). Under an 8,192-supervised-token windowed schedule, 9 of 12 runs halt under calibration drift or unresolved nonfinite training loss or gradients, leaving only full-cache replay completed at 0.7721. A repaired campaign with dynamic loss scaling halted at its learning-rate pilot under reference-solution loss drift before accessing the 346-problem locked test split. Because the gold-rationale positive control was never executed, these negative results cannot separate cache quality, selector quality, and learner-protocol limits. Our one positive finding separates parser repair from prompt changes on a 64-problem audit split: reparsing fixed base generations with a Decimal extractor raises parse rate from 0.8750 to 1.0000 and accuracy from 0.7344 to 0.8281, whereas appending a format suffix flips 0.2500 of canonical answers. A preregistered replication on 512 fresh GSM8K training problems reproduces this parser-only gain (+8.40 pp, 95% CI [+6.05, +10.94]) for this checkpoint. We contribute a ledger-traceable negative-result record and 9 lessons learned.

items.title: A comparison of knot point screening algorithms for highly adaptive lasso
items.summary: Highly adaptive lasso (HAL) is a nonparametric regression estimator with a rate of convergence $n^{-1/3}(\log n)^{d/2}$, where the data dimension $d$ only appears in the power of the log of sample size. This fast rate is crucial for many causal inference tasks, where efficient estimation typically requires nuisance parameters to be estimated at a specific rate. HAL achieves this rate and, when paired with semiparametrically efficient estimators -- such as those constructed using targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) -- can be used to develop efficient estimators. Beyond causal inference, HAL is applicable to a wide range of supervised machine learning tasks. The procedure for HAL involves first performing a basis expansion on the original design matrix $X$ and then computing a lasso solution path. Cross-validation is used to select the optimal $L_1$-norm for the coefficients. For datasets with all continuous covariates and no ties, the HAL design matrix can reach a dimension as large as $n \times n(2^d-1)$, imposing a significant computational and memory burden. To address this, screening algorithms are applied at both the variable and knot-point levels to make HAL practical for datasets of moderate to large sizes. In this work, we propose outcome-blind knot point screening based on center-based clustering -- $k$-means and partitioning around medoids (PAM) -- and compare it with the quantile-based screening implemented in the hal9001 R package at matched design-matrix sizes. Across 153 simulation settings, $k$-means and PAM significantly improved test $R^2$ in 97 and 111 settings, respectively, with gains that grow with covariate skewness, while producing slightly smaller design matrices. On nine real-world datasets, they reduced the cross-validated mean squared error by 35-36% on the dataset with the most skewed predictors and performed comparably on the others.

items.title: Sliced-Regularized Optimal Transport
items.summary: We propose a new regularized optimal transport (OT) formulation, termed sliced-regularized optimal transport (SROT). Unlike entropic OT (EOT), which regularizes the transport plan toward an independent coupling, SROT regularizes it toward a sliced OT (SOT) plan. To the best of our knowledge, SROT is the first approach to leverage a version of SOT plan as a reference to improve classical OT. We provide a formal definition of SROT, derive its dual formulation, and provide a post-Bayesian interpretation of SROT. We then develop a Sinkhorn-style algorithm for efficient computation. It retains the scalability of EOT and, when the SOT plan is sparse, achieves even lower per-iteration complexity. By incorporating a scalable SOT plan as a prior, SROT yields more accurate approximations of the exact OT plan than EOT under the same level of regularization. Moreover, the resulting transport plan improves upon the reference SOT plan itself. We further introduce the corresponding OT divergence induced by SROT, named SROT divergence, and analyze its topological and computational properties. Finally, we validate our approach through experiments on synthetic datasets and color transfer tasks, demonstrating that SROT is better than both EOT and SOT in approximating exact OT. Additional experiments on gradient flows further highlight the advantages of SROT divergence

items.title: Fuzzy e-Means: Fuzzy c-Means on Large Data with Moving-Average Mini-Batch Updates
items.summary: Fuzzy c-means (FCM) gives every point a degree of membership in every cluster. Its standard solver, alternating optimization (AO), needs a full pass over the data per iteration and often many iterations, while methods built for large data stop at a worse objective or still need tens of passes. We run FCM with the optimizer of e-means, a recent mini-batch k-means that keeps moving averages of the number and the sum of the points in each cluster and sets its batch size and step size by scaling laws. The optimizer carries over because an FCM centroid is also a weighted sum divided by a total weight, but this direct transfer fails in two ways: the e-means rule that relocates nearly empty clusters also removes the centroids of small, distant groups, and FCM started from random points can settle in poor local minima. Fuzzy e-means (e-FCM) therefore starts with one pass of e-means with hard assignments and then runs fuzzy moving-average passes without relocation. On 28 configurations with up to 109.5 million points and 16,384 clusters, e-FCM reaches the objective of 25 AO iterations in two to four passes when clusters hold several hundred points or more, 11 to 20 times faster than AO on one-million-point embedding sets with 1,024 clusters. It ends within 0.16% of converged AO on these sets and below converged AO where AO from random points lands in poor minima, but it is slower than AO on small low-dimensional problems, where an AO pass takes milliseconds. Finally, the common fuzzifier m=2 makes the centroids collapse or merge on most high-dimensional sets, and e-FCM can choose the fuzzifier by matching a known overlap at about two passes per candidate value.

items.title: Improving Efficiency and Power in Small Rare-Disease Trials Through Prespecified, Data-Adaptive Covariate Adjustment
items.summary: Covariate adjustment can potentially improve efficiency in randomized clinical trials, but in rare diseases, limited prior knowledge makes it difficult to specify an adjustment at the design stage. Targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) with the Super Learner (TMLE+SL) can outperform fixed adjustment methods, such as the G-computation estimator, by leveraging machine learning to learn both the covariates and the functional form of the adjustment from the trial data. Estimating the known treatment mechanism can improve efficiency further. In simulations reflecting real rare-disease trials, TMLE+SL yielded valid inference and achieved greater efficiency and power than conventional analyses. Finally, we also provide practical guidance on specifying TMLE+SL in rare-disease trials.

items.title: Fréchet Kriging for Metric Space-Valued Spatial Data
items.summary: Spatial prediction of non-Euclidean data, such as probability distributions, symmetric positive semidefinite matrices, and networks, arises in many modern applications. Such data are naturally modeled as elements of general metric spaces, where classical kriging methods that rely on vector space structure are no longer directly applicable. We introduce Fréchet kriging, a general framework for spatial prediction of metric space-valued data. Fréchet kriging replaces the weighted average in classical ordinary kriging with a weighted Fréchet mean, while the weights are determined by characterizing the spatial dependence structure through a generalized variogram. This construction allows the proposed method to preserve the intrinsic geometry of the response space without requiring an embedding into a linear space. We establish theoretical properties of the proposed predictor, including a surrogate optimality property and consistency under variogram misspecification. Simulation studies for univariate distributions and symmetric positive semidefinite matrices demonstrate favorable predictive performance compared with existing approaches. We further illustrate the practical utility of the proposed framework through applications to joint probability densities of daily minimum and maximum temperatures and inter-industry monetary flow networks.

items.title: Deep Negative Binomial Autoregression for Sparse Spatio-Temporal Counts: Estimation and Predictive Distribution Bounds
items.summary: We study estimation and probabilistic forecasting for sparse, overdispersed count panels using DeepNB-STAR, a negative binomial autoregression whose log-mean and log-size are outputs of a deep ReLU network of temporal and neighboring summaries of the past, fitted by maximum likelihood. We prove an oracle inequality for the Hellinger risk along the observed trajectory without mixing assumptions, rates governed by compositional smoothness with a matching lower bound for a Hölder subclass, geometric absolute regularity, and bounds on the error of h-step predictive distributions of order h^{1/2} times the root estimation risk plus a Monte Carlo term. All results hold for a size that depends on the covariates, and the estimation bounds hold under arbitrary dependence between sites, with the number of time points as sample size. On four Japanese surveillance panels, DeepNB-STAR has a weighted interval score 0.6% to 1.0% below that of a three-member ensemble of Temporal Fusion Transformers on every panel, distinguishable from zero only on the held-out panel. Fitted mean and size functions are reported with exploratory bootstrap intervals. Nominal 95% prediction intervals for national totals cover only 81% to 92% of weeks: the joint predictive law, unlike the estimator, relies on conditional independence across sites.

items.title: Why flattening the P-value histogram works: a theory of the standard-deviation optimization in tensor-decomposition-based unsupervised feature extraction
items.summary: Background: Tensor-decomposition-based unsupervised feature extraction (TD-based UFE) selects genes by attributing P-values to the components of a gene singular vector under a null normal distribution. The standard deviation sigma of this distribution is unknown and is chosen so that the histogram of the P-values of the genes that are not selected becomes as flat as possible. This heuristic has worked well in practice but has had no theoretical justification. Results: We prove, for a model of signal, mean expression and noise, that the higher-order singular value decomposition has a component that reproduces the experimental design, that the components of its gene singular vector belonging to background genes are approximately normal with standard deviation sigma_0 = sqrt(d)/s, where d is the noise variance and s the singular value, and that signal genes separate from the background even when they form a positive fraction of all genes. We derive the limit of the objective function of the flattening and prove, by a computer-assisted argument based on interval arithmetic, that for 100 histogram bins, Benjamini-Hochberg level 0.01 and every fraction of background genes between 0.1 and 0.99, the limit has a unique minimizer within 1.1% of sigma_0. We formalize the practice of taking the valley to the right of the peak of the objective as a maximum-drop rule and prove that the resulting estimator is consistent up to this bounded bias. Conclusions: Flattening the P-value histogram estimates the noise level of the background genes, with a small and bounded systematic bias, provided that the signals are strong enough to be detected individually and that the noise variances of background genes are nearly equal.

items.title: Model Selection and Averaging: Signal Strength, Ordering, and Oracle Risks
items.summary: Existing oracle risk comparisons of model selection (MS) and model averaging (MA) have primarily distinguished slowly and rapidly decaying ordered signal-importance sequences, leaving the comparison beyond these idealized but practically unrepresentative decay conditions insufficiently characterized. We revisit this problem for a complete nested collection of linear regression models with independent homoscedastic errors. Without prescribing a coefficient decay pattern, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the relative oracle gain of MA over MS to be asymptotically substantial or negligible. Under complete ordering of the coefficients, the determining quantity is the share of oracle MS risk contributed by components near the noise level. This characterization explains how the strengths and numbers of strong, moderate, and weak signals jointly affect the comparison. Under an arbitrary fixed ordering, a common pool-adjacent-violators partition represents both oracle risks and yields an analogous characterization through block averages and sizes. For application, we develop a consistent diagnostic under sub-Gaussian errors and suitable growth conditions, together with finite-sample confidence intervals under Gaussian errors. The Gaussian framework also provides confidence sets for a certain Rashomon set. Simulations and a diamond-price application illustrate the theoretical findings and the empirical assessment of the potential MA advantage.

items.title: Distribution-free predictive inference with instrumental variables
items.summary: We study the problem of predictive inference with outcomes missing not at random, when instrumental variables are available. While conformal prediction and weighted conformal prediction provide valid distribution-free inference when outcomes are missing completely at random and missing at random, respectively, inference is generally not possible without additional assumptions when outcomes are missing not at random. In this work, we consider a setting where we remain within the distribution-free framework but instead have access to an instrumental variable (IV). We explore the theoretical possibility of IV predictive inference and establish that it is characterized by a parameter that we refer to as the identification index. We derive an impossibility result for the case where the identification index is not sufficiently large, showing that any distribution-free approach fails to provide informative inference in this case. For the case where the identification index is sufficiently large, we introduce a practical method that achieves informative predictive inference. Our method leverages modern semiparametric efficiency theory which involves deriving the efficient influence function of the identifying functional for sharp IV bounds of the quantiles of the missing outcome, delivering a double robustness property in the coverage guarantee of the proposed framework for IV-based predictive inference. We illustrate the theoretical results and the performance of the proposed procedure through simulations and two real-data applications---FES wages and NHANES III self-reported heights.

items.title: ATLAS: Autoregressive Trajectories for Longitudinal Analysis of Survival
items.summary: Dynamic survival prediction requires estimates that reflect a patient's observed clinical history. We introduce ATLAS (Autoregressive Trajectories for Longitudinal Analysis of Survival), a framework that trains a sequence model on longitudinal data and autoregressively samples possible futures conditional on an individual's covariates and observed history. These trajectories form a patient-specific synthetic cohort from which Kaplan-Meier survival curves and Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence curves are estimated. We evaluate ATLAS using two stochastic finite-state automaton benchmarks with exact conditional reference curves: a single-covariate process with duration dependence and a late rule change, and a three-covariate Markov process with recovery and competing causes of death. Comparisons include eight direct survival models, including validation-optimized DRSA and Dynamic-DeepHit and history-aware SurvTRACE adaptations, with each neural model trained nine times in the first experiment and five times in the second. After baseline, every ATLAS configuration had lower mean survival-curve error than every fitted direct comparator in both experiments. With a common Sobol sampler and 10,000 trajectories per patient, the best ATLAS model did so in every individual training run, and its mean error was 62% to 84% lower than that of the strongest direct comparator. Baseline advantages were smaller and less consistent in the duration-dependent experiment. ATLAS provides a generative framework for history-conditioned survival estimation, while the accompanying benchmarks enable direct assessment of individual survival and competing-risk predictions against known reference curves.

items.title: Variance Reduction Based Experience Replay for Policy Optimization
items.summary: Effective reinforcement learning (RL) for complex stochastic systems requires leveraging historical data to improve sample efficiency and accelerate policy optimization. However, classical experience replay treats all past observations uniformly and fails to account for their varying contributions to learning. To address this limitation, we propose Variance Reduction Experience Replay (VRER), a principled framework that selectively reuses informative samples to reduce the variance of policy gradient estimates. VRER is algorithm-agnostic and can be integrated with existing policy optimization methods, yielding the sample-efficient off-policy algorithm, Policy Gradient with VRER (PG-VRER). To provide rigorous theoretical guarantees, we develop a novel analysis framework for experience replay that explicitly accounts for dependencies induced by Markovian dynamics and behavior-policy interactions. Using this framework, we establish finite-time convergence guarantees for PG-VRER and characterize a fundamental bias-variance trade-off: reusing older samples reduces gradient variance but may introduce greater estimation bias. Extensive experiments show that VRER consistently accelerates learning and outperforms state-of-the-art policy optimization algorithms

items.title: Counting Under Disagreement: Dollar-Weighted Measurement, Selective Machine Labelling and Budgeted Human Review from Disagreeing AI Readers of Administrative Text
items.summary: We study AI-assisted measurement when one text label applies to many administrative records, the target is a monetary total, and the human readings that anchor the machines disagree. The testbed is 121,070 grant-purpose texts from US tax filings (799,675 records, $126.4B), labelled by a rule-based classifier and three language models, with a designed sample of 651 texts read independently by three people under one codebook, who then adjudicated the 152 texts they split on. We state exact conditions for a fixed-predictor difference estimator and for a cross-fitted predictor whose folds are assigned to the whole frame independently of the sample, under Poisson sampling, and assess the implemented fixed-size procedures by simulation: 8 predictors whose own totals span $12.5-15.0B agree to within $0.4B once rectified. Two rules that accept machine labels at a stated dollar-weighted error, weighted conformal p-values under a dollar measure and Learn-then-Test on the design estimate of the error, are evaluated on nested held-out folds and on design re-draws with synthetic truths; their error control in deployment is not established, and the count-based rule accepts no text under a dollar-drawn sample. In a replay that counts every reference label a policy queries, pilot included (not the readings behind it), a two-phase review policy whose calibrator is fitted on its own first phase reduces the RMSE of the total by 42% at 100 queries relative to dollar-proportional sampling, while pure Neyman allocation fails with an uncalibrated predictor. Independent readers shift the estimated total by $3.93B, 2.7 times the sampling interval; the adjudicated reading puts it at $13.49B; institution-level intervals under-cover at every size. Reference-dependent results are re-run under each reader. The results identify benefits and limits of using learned predictions to decide what a person should verify.

items.title: Fold Weighting for Cross-Validation Under Continuous Distributional Drift
items.summary: Cross-validation weights all folds equally, so under drift the oldest folds count as much as the newest. We model drift by a Hölder condition in total variation distance and give finite-sample bounds on the excess deployment risk of the configuration that sliding-window cross-validation selects. Each bound splits into drift, estimation, and validation-noise terms. With equal weights the drift terms saturate as the record grows. With fold weights fixed in advance, the drift terms become weighted averages, which shrink as weight moves toward deployment. The noise term grows as the weights concentrate and shrinks with the batch size. The drift terms are linear in the weights and the noise term is convex, so minimizing the bound over the weights is a convex problem. Applications to U.S. earnings and flight delays show both sides of this trade-off. Weight on recent folds pays off when a change in the best predictor persists and each period has many observations, and equal weights do best when changes are short-lived.

items.title: Second-Order Response Laws for LLM Judges:From Prompt Stability to Decision Quality
items.summary: LLM judges are used to compare models and select responses, yet a judge can change its verdict when a prompt is reworded. The change may come from the wording or from the randomness of another call. Confusing the two can distort model comparisons and response selection, but they are hard to separate with few repeated calls, and plug-in prompt-dispersion scores mix them. We develop a framework that connects measurements of judge variability to decision quality. It rests on second-order response laws, which describe how verdict distributions vary across prompts. Crossing prompts with candidate orders separates prompt, position, interaction, and call variation, and agreement between distinct calls removes the finite-call bias. We derive the corrected estimator's exact variance and matching bounds for detecting weak prompt effects under a fixed, balanced design. In over one million judgments from six judges on three benchmarks, the correction changes conclusions. On a matched panel, it reverses the estimated Qwen--Gemma-3 ranking by prompt sensitivity. Lowering the sampling temperature (cooling) makes Qwen's calls more consistent while its corrected prompt estimate rises nearly fivefold (call-level interval 3.3 to 8.5), a rise the plug-in estimate misses. Pre-specified studies on 320 unseen items and 24 unseen prompts confirm the increase. In votes balanced across candidate orders, cooling produces more ties in Qwen, and changing only the tie rule shifts the estimated accuracy effect of cooling by 9.84 percentage points. An analytical model shows how position dependence can push such votes toward ties and lower accuracy under abstention even when the judge favors the correct answer. The value of consistency therefore depends on alignment with correct answers, the voting rule, and the cost of abstention.

items.title: Sub-Gaussian HDLSS Principal Component Analysis: High-Probability Theory and Numerical Evidence for NRM, CDM, and Block Noise Reduction
items.summary: We study principal component analysis when the dimension d is much larger than the sample size n under an independent-factor sub-Gaussian model. The dual sample covariance is decomposed into a finite-rank score matrix, an isotropic bulk shift, and a high-probability remainder governed by the bulk trace τ_0, Frobenius scale q_0, and largest noise eigenvalue b_0 = ||Λ_0||_{op}. This decomposition separates fixed-score HDLSS limits from joint limits in which n also grows. It shows that sequential noise reduction generally targets a score oracle containing a later-spike subtraction, while an oracle block correction avoids that subtraction when the signal rank is known. A parallel cross-data-matrix bound explains the benefit and cost of sample splitting. Reproducible Gaussian-factor simulations with 1,000 replications per configuration confirm the score-oracle approximation, the multi-spike subtraction, the separation between eigenvalue and eigenvector scales, and the population transition when n grows.

items.title: Mirror Descent at the Edge of Stability
items.summary: In many deep learning settings, gradient descent has been shown to operate at the edge of stability -- a regime where the largest eigenvalue of the loss Hessian hovers around $2/η$. We study this phenomenon in mirror descent, a generalization of gradient descent. As mirror descent is non-Euclidean, existing explanations of the edge of stability phase do not extend to this setting. We generalize the existing notion of sharpness to introduce mirror sharpness, which measures the curvature of the loss with respect to the mirror potential. Empirically, we observe that the mirror sharpness hovers slightly above the $2/η$ threshold. Furthermore, we derive a dual central flow ODE for mirror descent that models iterates in continuous time at the onset of edge of stability. Our ODE provides insights into the difficulties of extending existing arguments for why sharpness stabilizes at $2/η$ from gradient descent to mirror descent in full generality.

items.title: A Calculus Gradient: Child Poverty, Mathematics Preparation, and First-Year College Performance at a Hispanic-Serving University
items.summary: The San Antonio metropolitan area has one of the highest poverty rates among large U.S. metropolitan areas. Within Bexar County, where the city is located, child poverty varies widely across school districts. We link entrants of the city's public research university, a broad-access Hispanic-Serving Institution, to their sending schools and districts, and examine their preparation scores and first-year outcomes. Across the nation's school districts, enrollment in widely taken core courses (Algebra II, Geometry, Biology) shows little relation to child poverty, while enrollment in Calculus and Advanced Placement mathematics and science is far lower where child poverty is higher, nationally and within Bexar County. Among linked entrants, mathematics preparation differs with the school and district. Entrants with stronger mathematics preparation earn higher first-year grades in nearly every subject. Most entrants who do not return after the first year had unsuccessful courses, and mathematics is the largest single source of those outcomes. Among students who change major, mathematics is one of the subjects with grades furthest below their own averages. Within the same course and term, larger mathematics sections go with more unsuccessful outcomes for entrants with lower mathematics preparation, which identifies a hypothesis for testing smaller sections. Recorded between Fall 2014 and Fall 2019, these outcomes offer a reference point for change after the pandemic, test-optional admissions, and generative artificial intelligence. The analysis is reproducible; adapting it elsewhere requires local definitions and linkage validation. All results are associations among the students of one institution; establishing causes would require a designed study.

items.title: Individualized Prediction Bands in Causal Inference with Continuous Treatments
items.summary: Individualized treatments are crucial for optimal decision-making and treatment allocation, specifically in personalized medicine based on the estimation of an individual's dose-response curve across a continuum of treatment levels, e.g., drug dosage. Current works focus on conditional mean and median estimates, which are useful but do not provide the full picture. We propose viewing causal inference with a continuous treatment as a covariate shift. This allows us to leverage existing weighted conformal prediction methods with both quantile and point estimates to compute individualized uncertainty quantification for dose-response curves. When used with quantile regression, our method, individualized prediction bands (IPB), enjoys a doubly robust coverage property. We demonstrate IPB via simulations and a real data analysis that assesses the additional medical expenditure caused by continued smoking for selected individuals. Our results show that IPB provides an effective solution to a gap in the individual dose-response uncertainty quantification literature.

items.title: Multilevel non-linear interrupted time series analysis
items.summary: Recent advances in interrupted time series analysis permit characterization of a typical non-linear interruption effect through use of generalized additive models. Concurrently, advances in latent time series modeling allow efficient Bayesian multilevel time series models. We propose to combine these concepts with a hierarchical model selection prior to characterize interruption effects with a multilevel structure, encouraging parsimony and partial pooling while incorporating meaningful variability in causal effects across subpopulations of interest, while allowing poststratification. These models are demonstrated with three applications: 1) the effect of the introduction of the prostate specific antigen test on prostate cancer diagnosis rates by race and age group, 2) the change in stroke or trans-ischemic attack hospitalization rates across Medicare beneficiaries by rurality in the months after the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, and 3) the effect of Medicaid expansion in Missouri on the proportion of inpatient hospitalizations discharged with Medicaid as a primary payer by key age groupings and sex.

items.title: Proxy-Based Approximation of Shapley and Banzhaf Interactions
items.summary: Shapley and Banzhaf interactions capture the complex dynamics inherent in modern machine learning applications. However, current estimators for these higher-order interactions trade off between speed and accuracy. To overcome this limitation, we introduce ProxySHAP. ProxySHAP reconciles the high sample efficiency of tree-based proxy models with a situational residual correction recovering consistency. On a theoretical level, we derive a polynomial-time generalization of interventional TreeSHAP that computes exact interaction indices for tree ensembles, thereby bypassing exponential tree-depth dependencies in prior methods. Furthermore, we formally analyze the residual adjustment strategy, characterizing the specific conditions under which Maximum Sample Reuse (MSR) corrects proxy bias without its variance scaling exponentially with interaction size. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates that ProxySHAP sets a new state-of-the-art standard for approximation quality, including in large-scale applications with thousands of features. By achieving the lowest error in both small- and large-budget regimes, ProxySHAP significantly outperforms the prior best estimators ProxySPEX and KernelSHAP-IQ, while also delivering superior performance on downstream explainability tasks.

items.title: Zero-Shot Prognostic Covariate Adjustment and Mechanistic Week-1 Myelosuppression Updating Across 9,500 Oncology Patients Under FDA Guidance
items.summary: The FDA's 2023 guidance on covariate adjustment recommends "that sponsors adjust for covariates that are anticipated to be most strongly associated with the outcome of interest" and notes that "it may be useful to use previous studies (e.g. a Phase 2 trial) to select prognostic covariates or form prognostic indices." Its August 2024 guidance on dosage optimization, part of Project Optimus, states that "the dose- and exposure-response relationships should be evaluated to select a dosage(s) for clinical trial(s)." We analyzed the control arms of 14 randomized trials from Project Data Sphere, with 5,074 patients with overall survival follow-up, in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC), and in three AACR Project GENIE Biopharma Collaborative cohorts (4,440 patients). In all, about 9,500 patients were studied. We used the regularized baseline prognostic index to compute out-of-fold estimates of the share of covariate-adjusted log-rank variance removed ($ρ^2$), and found these to be 0.177 to 0.186 for the three indications. For the locked held-out trials, the value was 0.183 (second-line NSCLC docetaxel), 0.177 (first-line PDAC gemcitabine) and 0.110 (first-line mCRC FOLFOX plus bevacizumab). Refitting in GENIE BPC resulted in estimates of 0.073 to 0.127 for first-line and 0.122 to 0.219 for later lines. In a simulated 600-patient trial, 5,000 within-stratum re-randomizations gave a type I error rate of 0.051 for the adjusted test. At $ρ^2 = 0.18$, adjustment raises power from 80.0% to 87.2%, cuts required events by 18% or shrinks the control arm by about 30%. A Friberg marrow prior updated with week 1 blood counts raised the AUROC for new cycle 1 grade 3 or worse neutropenia from 0.791 to 0.816 (n = 3,465; calibration slope 0.999; Brier skill 0.190) and raised it in 5 of 8 cross-trial rows (up to +0.116).

items.title: Stochastic non-metric MDS for noisy high-dimensional data
items.summary: Multidimensional scaling (MDS) constructs low-dimensional embeddings that approximate pairwise distances in a high-dimensional dataset. MDS exists in several flavors, with metric MDS approximating distances directly and non-metric MDS additionally optimizing for an arbitrary monotonic transformation of the high-dimensional distances. Empirically, metric MDS is known to suffer from the curse of dimensionality. Here we extend prior theoretical results for metric MDS on fully uninformative data to a more general case of finite, high-dimensional data with concentrated distances. We show that the metric MDS embeddings of such datasets stay distributionally close to the data-independent limit case. We then show that non-metric MDS is more robust to high-dimensional noise and can yield informative embeddings of such data. While existing implementations of non-metric MDS are slow, we develop a fast implementation using stochastic gradient descent in PyTorch. Using our implementation, we conduct an empirical study using multiple simulated and real-world datasets, including population-genomic and scRNA-seq data, and show that non-metric MDS can strongly outperform other methods in terms of global structure preservation.

items.title: Robust Pair--Restricted Lipschitz Regression with Global--Local Transfer
items.summary: We develop a robust pair-restricted Lipschitz regression framework for grouped longitudinal data represented as finite trajectories in a space equipped with a prescribed or learned pseudometric. For a fixed geometry, latent responses and a Lipschitz bound are estimated jointly through a convex optimisation problem with constraints imposed on selected trajectory pairs. We show that the choice of fidelity loss leads to different structural behaviour: Huber regularisation strictly reduces the pair-restricted Lipschitz seminorm whenever the exact interpolant has a finite positive seminorm, whereas $L^1$ fidelity can preserve exact interpolation below a data-dependent threshold. For grouped observations, global and local Lipschitz structures are combined while keeping group identity outside the trajectory geometry. The global component draws on observations from other groups, while the local component uses each group's history to account for group-specific behaviour. We also characterise when group-specific observations can be fitted exactly under a shared Lipschitz bound and establish a regularity bound for the combined predictor. We describe a computational implementation based on constraint generation and illustrate the framework through an application to longitudinal sow-production data.

items.title: Kemeny median rankings with ties under constraints on the buckets
items.summary: The median ranking is the ranking that minimizes the sum of the Kemeny distances from the rankings expressed by a set of judges. In many applications the consensus requires a prescribed structure: a given number of buckets, given sizes of all or some of the buckets, as in the forced distributions of Q methodology, or the form of a top-$k$ list. We show that all these problems are a single problem, the search for the median ranking among the rankings whose pattern of bucket sizes is admissible, and that they depend on the data only through the combined input matrix, defined by Emond and Mason in 2002. On this matrix we build BOLT, a deterministic heuristic that combines a set of starting solutions, a local search that moves one object at a time and can create or remove ties, and the exact best partition of a fixed order of the objects into buckets with an admissible pattern. We also provide an exact solution for the median top-$k$ list. The solutions of BOLT are assessed, on real and simulated data, against the optimum certified by a binary linear programming formulation, adapted to the Kemeny distance and to the constraints on the buckets, and against the methods available in the literature. Applications to Q-sorts, top-$k$ lists and large and sparse data sets of ratings show how the constrained problems arise in practice, and how the treatment of the objects not ranked by the judges changes the solution.

items.title: Religious expression and well-being across countries and regions: Evidence from a decade of social media posts
items.summary: This study examines whether social connectedness constitutes a pathway between religious expression and subsequent well-being. Drawing on millions of social-media posts, we combine broad international coverage, subnational geographic detail, and annual observations over 2013-2022 to examine religious expression, connectedness, and three well-being dimensions. The longitudinal models account for baseline connectedness and well-being, geographic and year effects, and national trends. National longitudinal models support positive indirect associations through social connectedness for happiness and life satisfaction. The indirect estimates for purpose nationally and for all three outcomes regionally are positive but imprecise. Complementary coefficient contrasts in contemporaneous regional models and comparisons of regional period averages show stronger associations of religious expression with purpose than with either happiness or life satisfaction. Together, these findings support a national pathway through social connectedness for the affective and evaluative dimensions of well-being. The stronger regional associations with purpose motivate further investigation of meaning- and direction-related processes beyond the measured connectedness pathway.

items.title: Adaptive Two-Sample Testing for Regression Discrepancy and Model Misspecification in High Dimensions
items.summary: In two-sample regression comparisons, testing for equality is often too restrictive because minor discrepancies in functional form are unavoidable in practice. We study whether the functional discrepancy falls within a practically acceptable tolerance. Such tolerance-based comparison can, however, be unreliable when either regression model is misspecified. To address both issues, we propose a unified adaptive-to-model testing framework for high-dimensional regressions that integrates model checking with functional similarity testing for the two populations. For functional similarity, we develop an adaptive boundary-proxy test whose rejection probability converges to the nominal level at every fixed configuration of the composite null hypothesis, overcoming the conservatism of conventional least favorable configuration tests. For model misspecification, we use projection-based tests for sparse high-dimensional regression models. These components are combined through adaptive gating into a joint test. We investigate its asymptotic null distribution and power properties under global and local alternatives. Numerical studies examine its finite-sample performance.

items.title: A Novel Approach to Clustering Shape Data Using Iteratively Weighted Vectors with k-Means
items.summary: Topological data analysis provides a collection of methods for analyzing data with shape structure, including point clouds, graphs, and images. Recent advances in topological vectorization have enabled the embedding of shape data into Euclidean spaces, facilitating comparisons and machine learning tasks. Vector summaries that effectively capture topological structures are particularly useful for shape classification and unsupervised learning tasks such as clustering. We investigate the use of vectorized topological data for clustering through k-means, which partitions observations into a fixed number of groups by minimizing a squared-error loss function. By incorporating an element-wise weight-update step into the iterative k-means algorithm, we improve clustering performance on both simulated and real-world shape datasets. We show that estimating these weights reduces to a least-squares problem, requiring minimal additional computation while allowing flexible coefficient constraints. Our approach also substantially strengthens the negative correlation between the loss and clustering accuracy, improving the effectiveness of selecting among multiple clustering solutions based on the lowest loss. These improvements remain robust to changes in vector length and the number of initializations. Furthermore, weighted topological vector summaries exhibit stability under small structural perturbations, particularly when weight constraints are imposed. The proposed method offers a flexible alternative for clustering topological data, accommodating different k-means variants, vectorization methods, and weight constraints.

items.title: Correlation-aware sequential sampling for multi-output polynomial chaos expansions
items.summary: The interaction of multiple physical processes in complex engineering systems is often characterized by several quantities of interest (QoIs) with non-negligible cross-correlations. Accurate uncertainty quantification of these responses requires repeated model evaluations, which can be computationally expensive. As an alternative, polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) provides an efficient surrogate modeling framework for reducing this computational cost owing to its natural structure for statistical analysis, while adaptive sequential sampling can further improve sampling efficiency under a limited model evaluation budget. However, adaptive sampling strategies specifically designed for multi-output PCE remain limited, and existing approaches commonly aggregate information from individual outputs without explicitly accounting for their statistical dependence. When strong correlations exist among QoIs, output-wise aggregation can give greater combined influence to response patterns shared by several outputs. To reduce the influence of such repeated representation on sample allocation, this study develops a principal component analysis-based extension of the multi-output criterion for adaptive construction of PCE. The sampling criterion combines component-wise normalization with the retention of selected principal directions, thereby adjusting the relative influence of shared response patterns while preserving distance-based exploration. The method is verified through numerical examples with different levels of output coupling and is compared with the conventional multi-output criterion and reference sampling strategies. The results demonstrate that accounting for output dependence improves the allocation of new samples among multiple response features and enhances the efficiency of multi-output PCE surrogate construction, particularly for strongly correlated QoIs.

items.title: Fast likelihood evaluation for multivariate sensory discrimination models
items.summary: Sensory discrimination is often measured by fitting statistical models with likelihood functions that are computationally challenging to evaluate. In the standard triangle and duo-trio tests, a subject is presented with three stimuli, two of one kind and one of another, and is asked to identify the odd one out (the triangle test) or which of two stimuli matches a reference (the duo-trio test). In a Thurstonian model, the subject's internal representation of each stimulus is a Gaussian whose mean and covariance depend on the stimulus, and the probability that the subject's response is correct is an integral over a $3d$-dimensional Gaussian with no closed form for $d > 1$, where $d$ is the dimension of the stimulus space. To fit a statistical model to data collected from triangle or duo-trio tests, the likelihood function, and often its gradient, need to be evaluated many times, making statistical inference inefficient. Here, we introduce fast algorithms for evaluating certain classes of likelihood functions for the triangle and duo-trio tests. The algorithms rely on reducing the dimension of these functions. The triangle probability, a function of $2d + d(d+1)$ arguments, reduces analytically to a function of $2d$ arguments, and the duo-trio probability, when the two stimuli have equal covariances, reduces to a function of a single scalar for any $d$. After reducing the dimensionality of those functions, we use neural networks and Chebyshev expansions to evaluate the lower-dimensional functions efficiently. Our algorithms demonstrate orders of magnitude speedups over existing approaches at comparable accuracy, both for a single evaluation and when used to compute the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate of a model of color discrimination. The dimensionality reduction we use generalizes to non-Gaussian noise models with elliptical level sets, and to tests with more than three stimuli.

items.title: Twisted Block Particle Filters: A Local Particle-System Change of Measure for High-Dimensional State-Space Models
items.summary: Block particle filters mitigate weight degeneracy in high-dimensional state-space models, but their normalizer estimates can remain highly variable. We introduce a twisted block particle filter (TBPF) that incorporates predictive guidance through an exact change of measure at blockwise resampling. The method guide-tilts one uniformly selected offspring per block, leaves the state-transition kernel unchanged, and computes the resampling correction using finite empirical guide averages. We prove that this correction exactly preserves the finite-particle block particle filter normalizer expectation, separating the effect of guided sampling from the approximation introduced by spatial blocking. Our analysis provides exact conditional local moments and a one-step conditional central limit result. We further derive explicit bounds on the correction accumulated across blocks and time, establish fixed-horizon consistency of the block filter and corrected normalizer under suitable regularity and guide-range conditions, and identify conditional criteria for guide perturbations that reduce variance. Experiments on coupled linear Gaussian and stochastic-volatility models with up to 256 latent dimensions show lower measured log-normalizer variance. For stochastic volatility with a five-step guide, the median reduction is $38\%$. An application to a 100-dimensional financial portfolio panel extends the evaluation to real data.

items.title: Convergence of Large-Stepsize SGD for the Cross-entropy Loss via Stochastic Lyapunov Stability
items.summary: Modern deep learning has been shown to operate using learning rates far larger than those justified by classical optimization theory. Most prior analyses of this phenomenon focus on deterministic gradient descent, leaving the stochastic setting largely unexplored. In this work, we provide sharp convergence guarantees for Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) applied to the multiclass cross-entropy loss, for both linear classifiers and two-layer neural networks. We show that the stochasticity of SGD may cause the dynamics to alternate between an edge-of-stability regime that is dominated by curvature-driven oscillations, and a stable regime in which the expected loss decreases at a controlled rate. Despite that, we prove that SGD stabilizes the dynamics, ensuring that the iterates return to stability in a fixed number of iterations and allowing convergence in the best-iterate sense even with large learning rates. Experiments validate our theoretical findings and illustrate the benefits of SGD in the large-stepsize regime.

items.title: Quadruply robust methods for causal mediation analysis
items.summary: Estimating natural effects is a core task in causal mediation analysis. Existing triply robust (TR) frameworks (Tchetgen Tchetgen & Shpitser 2012) and their extensions have been developed to estimate the natural effects. In this work, we introduce a new quadruply robust (QR) framework that enlarges the model class for unbiased identification. We study two modeling strategies. The first is a nonparametric modeling approach, under which we propose a general QR estimator that supports the use of machine learning methods for nuisance estimation. We also study high-dimensional settings, where the dimensions of covariates and mediators may both be large. In these settings, we adopt a parametric modeling strategy and develop a model quadruply robust (MQR) estimator to limit the impact of model misspecification. Simulation studies and a real data application demonstrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed methods.

items.title: Censored Regression Models with Endogeneity: A Survey
items.summary: This survey article provides a comprehensive overview of methodologies developed to handle endogeneity in censored regression models. We emphasize their theoretical basis, and estimating methodologies. The paper summarizes the benefits and drawbacks of each technique and addresses expansions to nonlinear, panel, and high-dimensional settings, offering researchers practical assistance and identifying options for future methodological improvement in censored models with endogenous regressors.

items.title: Exact Algebraic Computation of Learning Coefficients for Two-Dimensional Singular Models
items.summary: Classical information criteria such as the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) rely on regularity assumptions that break down for singular models, leading to incorrect model selection in settings such as deep learning. The Widely Applicable Bayesian Information Criterion (WBIC) relies on local learning coefficients $λ$, which in the analytic case coincides with local Real Log Canonical Thresholds (RLCT) of the Kullback-Leibler divergence of the model, to capture correct marginal likelihood asymptotics. Exact computation of the learning coefficients has been limited to special cases, and only sampling-based estimation methods are generally applicable. We present the first deterministic algorithm that computes local RLCTs exactly for any two-dimensional model whose Kullback-Leibler distance is contact equivalent to a polynomial, derive a bound on its complexity, and demonstrate its effectiveness for a broad class of models, with applications including polynomial neural networks. Beyond providing ground truth to calibrate sampling-based estimators, exact computation reveals algebraic structure in learning coefficients that sampling cannot and out-speeds it in the shallow regime.

items.title: Automated Techniques for Efficient Sampling of Piecewise-Deterministic Markov Processes
items.summary: Piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) are a class of continuous-time Markov processes that have recently been used to develop a new class of Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms. However, implementing these processes is challenging because of their continuous-time nature and the need to integrate the rate function. Recently, Corbella, Spencer, and Roberts (2022) proposed a new algorithm that automates the implementation of the Zig-Zag sampler. However, the efficiency of the algorithm depends strongly on a hyperparameter ($t_{\mathrm{max}}$) that remains fixed throughout the run and must be tuned through preliminary runs. In this work, we relax this constraint and propose a new variant of the algorithm that allows this parameter to change over time and adapt automatically to the target distribution. We also replace Brent's optimization algorithm with a grid-based method for computing an upper bound on the rate function. This method is more robust to irregularities in the function and produces a tighter upper bound more quickly. We also extend the algorithm to other PDMPs and provide a Python implementation based on JAX.

items.title: Cure-Fraction Random Survival Forests: Separating Cure from Latency
items.summary: In many cancer and clinical studies, the population under study has a positive fraction of long-term survivors, motivating survival models that distinguish probability of long-term survival (cure fraction) from the latency of the subgroup that is susceptible to the event. Existing survival trees and forests partition data using criteria that emphasize differences in the ranks of survival times and therefore need not identify covariates associated with cure probability. We introduce cure-fraction based survival trees (CBST) that recursively partition the covariate space using contrasts in tail survival probability supported by adequate follow-up. The resulting ensemble forest targets long-term survival heterogeneity directly rather than ranking of the survival times. We establish consistency for the induced tail-survival target and derive conditions under which our procedure consistently recovers cure-rate related partitions and cure probabilities. The analysis clarifies the separate roles of follow-up maturity, localization, and residual-tail bias in identifying cure effects and supporting statistical inference. We further develop variance estimation and asymptotic results and uncertainty quantification for predictions from the ensemble forest.
